orig_9709_s1_var_raw_moments.description: A centre does not describe the whole distribution. Use ordered values to find range and IQR, use all deviations to measure variance, and distinguish the data’s spread from distances measured around another reference.

sections.title: What do range and IQR measure?
sections.label: Range and quartiles
sections.intro:
A centre tells you where a dataset lies, but not how tightly its values cluster. The range uses the two extremes; the interquartile range describes the gap between the lower and upper quartiles:

\[\text{range}=\max(x)-\min(x),\qquad\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1.\]

Both use the original measurement units. Range responds directly to an extreme endpoint. IQR is less sensitive to changes far out in the tails, although changing the count or ordering can change the quartile positions.

blocks.html: Raw quartiles in this course: sort the observations and retain repeats. Find the overall median. For an odd count, exclude only that one middle observation when forming the halves. For an even count, split all records into equal halves without removing the two middle observations. \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are the medians of those halves. Follow a different rule if a question explicitly supplies one.

In order, the records are \(4,6,7,9,10,12,14,16,18,30\). The middle position in each half gives its quartile.

\[Q_2=\frac{10+12}2=11,\qquad\mathrm{IQR}=16-7=9,\qquad\mathrm{range}=30-4=26.\]

All ten observations belong to the two halves. Their middle values give \(Q_1=7\) and \(Q_3=16\), so \(\mathrm{IQR}=9\).

blocks.title: Exclude one position, not every equal value
blocks.prompt:
Find the median, quartiles, range and IQR of

\[5,7,7,9,9,10,13,15,29.\]

Use the median-of-halves convention: for this odd count, exclude only the single overall middle observation when forming the two halves. Retain every other record, including equal values.
blocks.hint: The overall median is the fifth observation. The earlier record with the same value still belongs to the lower half.
blocks.solution:
1. The overall median is \(9\) at position \(5\). The two halves are

    \[(5,7,7,9)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(10,13,15,29).\]
  2. \[Q_1=\frac{7+7}{2}=7,\qquad Q_3=\frac{13+15}{2}=14.\]
  3. \[\text{range}=29-5=24,\qquad\mathrm{IQR}=14-7=7.\]

blocks.html: The quartile interval describes central spread; with finite samples and ties, it need not contain exactly half the observed values. Grouped cumulative-frequency estimates use a separate interpolation method, not this raw-list convention.

sections.title: How do all observations contribute to variance?
sections.label: Centred deviations
sections.intro:
For \(n\) numerical observations with mean \(\mu\), a deviation is \(x-\mu\). Positive and negative deviations sum to zero, so square them before adding:

\[D=\sum(x-\mu)^2,\qquad\sigma^2=\frac{D}{n},\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.\]

\(D\) is the centred sum of squares. Descriptive variance is its average over all \(n\) records, using \(n>0\). Every observation contributes, including repeats and extremes.

blocks.html: Use deviations from the actual mean and the descriptive divisor \(n\). Variance has squared units; SD has the original units. For lengths in centimetres, these are \(\mathrm{cm}^2\) and \(\mathrm{cm}\), respectively.
Variance and SD cannot be negative. They are zero exactly when all observations have the same value; that value need not be zero. A single-observation dataset therefore has zero descriptive variance.

blocks.title: Signed deviations can cancel while their squares do not
blocks.prompt: Four signed measurement errors, in centimetres, are \(-4,-1,2,3\). Find their mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation. What would a descriptive SD of zero imply for any nonempty dataset?

options.equal: All observations are equal, although their common value need not be zero.
options.sum: The signed observations add to zero.

blocks.hint: Find the mean before calculating deviations. Squaring prevents positive and negative deviations from cancelling.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=\frac{-4-1+2+3}{4}=0\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
  2. \[D=(-4)^2+(-1)^2+2^2+3^2=30\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  3. \[\sigma^2=\frac{30}{4}=\frac{15}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}^2,\qquad\sigma=\frac{\sqrt{30}}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  4. A sum of non-negative squared deviations is zero only when every deviation is zero. Therefore all observations must equal their common mean.

blocks.html: For comparisons, explain both centre and spread in context. Mean and SD use all records; median and IQR describe the centre and spread with less sensitivity to extreme magnitudes. A smaller spread means more consistent observed values, not automatically a better outcome for every purpose.

sections.title: Can I find variance from totals alone?
sections.label: Moment formulas
sections.intro:
Write \(T=\sum x\), \(Q=\sum x^2\), and \(\mu=\frac{T}{n}\). Expanding the centred squares gives

\[D=\sum(x-\mu)^2=Q-2\mu T+n\mu^2=Q-\frac{T^2}{n}.\]

Therefore either route gives the same descriptive variance:

\[\sigma^2=\frac{D}{n}=\frac{Q}{n}-\left(\frac{T}{n}\right)^2.\]

blocks.html: On a calculator, select the population or descriptive SD calculation, which uses divisor \(n\). Show \(n,T,Q\) and the substitution in your written solution. Keep the sum of squares \(Q\) separate from the square of the total \(T^2\). Retain full precision until the final result. Exact valid totals must satisfy \(Q\ge\frac{T^2}{n}\), because \(D\ge0\). An exact negative result signals inconsistent data or a calculation error; do not replace it with zero.

blocks.title: Check whether exact moment totals are possible
blocks.prompt: Four masses, in grams, have total \(T=28\,\mathrm{g}\) and sum of squares \(Q=220\,\mathrm{g}^2\). Find the mean, centred sum of squares and descriptive variance. A separate proposal has the same count and total but \(Q=190\,\mathrm{g}^2\). Could those proposed exact totals describe real observations?

options.no: No: its implied centred sum of squares is negative.
options.yes: Yes: a variance can be negative when values are below the mean.
options.zero: Yes: replace its negative variance by zero.

blocks.hint: Use \(D=Q-\frac{T^2}{n}\). A genuine centred sum of squares cannot be negative.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=\frac{28}{4}=7\,\mathrm{g},\qquad D=220-\frac{28^2}{4}=24\,\mathrm{g}^2.\]
  2. \[\sigma^2=\frac{24}{4}=6\,\mathrm{g}^2.\]

  3. The separate proposal would give

    \[D=190-\frac{28^2}{4}=190-196=-6\,\mathrm{g}^2.\]

    This is impossible. With that count and total, the sum of squares must be at least \(196\,\mathrm{g}^2\).

sections.title: Why does the mean give the smallest squared-distance total?
sections.label: Choosing a reference
sections.intro:
Keep the observations fixed and choose any real reference \(a\). Write \(S(a)=\sum(x-a)^2\). Using \(x-a=(x-\mu)+(\mu-a)\), the cross term disappears because \(\sum(x-\mu)=0\). This gives

\[S(a)=\sum(x-\mu)^2+n(a-\mu)^2=D+n(a-\mu)^2.\]

The extra square is non-negative and vanishes only at \(a=\mu\). Thus the minimum sum of squares is \(D=n\sigma^2\), while the minimum average squared distance is \(\sigma^2\). Neither is zero unless all original observations are equal.

blocks.title: Minimise distances without changing the observations
blocks.prompt: The fixed observations are \(1,3,7,9\). Define \(S(a)=\sum(x-a)^2\), where \(a\) is any real reference value. Find the reference that minimises \(S\), the minimum value, the original descriptive variance, and every real \(a\) for which \(S(a)=56\).
blocks.hint: Find the true mean and centred sum of squares first. Then use the reference-point identity and keep both roots of the squared equation.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=\frac{1+3+7+9}{4}=5,\qquad D=(-4)^2+(-2)^2+2^2+4^2=40.\]
  2. \[S(a)=40+4(a-5)^2.\]

    The unique minimum is \(40\), at \(a=5\). The original variance is \(\frac{40}{4}=10\).

  3. \[40+4(a-5)^2=56\Longrightarrow(a-5)^2=4.\]\[a=5\pm2,\qquad a\in\{3,7\}.\]

  4. Both reference values give the stated sum of squares. Neither choice changes the original records or their variance.

blocks.html: Moving the reference changes the distances being measured; it leaves the records and their variance fixed. For a prescribed sum of squares, solve the resulting squared equation completely. If an additional interval or integer restriction on \(a\) is stated, apply it to every resulting value.

glossary.definition: The largest observation minus the smallest observation.
The raw-data convention used here: find each half’s median, excluding only the single overall middle observation when the full count is odd.
The gap \(Q_3-Q_1\) between the upper and lower quartiles.
The signed difference \(x-\mu\) from the actual mean.
The total \(D=\sum(x-\mu)^2\), before dividing by the count.
The average squared deviation, \(\sigma^2=\frac{D}{n}\), also written \(V\).
The non-negative square root of the variance, expressed in the original measurement units.
The total \(T=\sum x\) and sum of squares \(Q=\sum x^2\), used to recover the mean and variance.
A chosen value \(a\) from which distances are measured, without changing the original records.
How closely the recorded values cluster; a statement about the available data rather than a guarantee about future observations.

examples.title: Split an even list into equal halves
examples.question:
For the ordered data below, find the median, quartiles, range and IQR. Use the median-of-halves convention; with an even count, retain all observations in two equal halves.

\[4,6,7,9,10,12,14,16,18,30.\]

Then explain what changes if the final observation \(30\) is replaced by \(60\).
solution:
There are ten observations. The median is the average of the values at positions \(5\) and \(6\):

\[\text{median}=\frac{10+12}{2}=11.\]

The lower half is \(4,6,7,9,10\); its middle value is \(7\). The upper half is \(12,14,16,18,30\); its middle value is \(16\). Thus

\[Q_1=7,\qquad Q_3=16.\]

Replacing only the final value by \(60\) gives range \(60-4=56\). The median and both half-medians remain at the same unchanged records, so the IQR remains \(9\). This conclusion uses the unchanged order and count in this particular edit.

examples.title: Square deviations from the actual mean
examples.question: Calculate the descriptive variance and standard deviation of the numerical observations \(2,5,5,8\), showing the deviations from their mean.
solution:
\(x\)\(x-\mu\)\((x-\mu)^2\)
\(2\)\(-3\)\(9\)
\(5\)\(0\)\(0\)
\(5\)\(0\)\(0\)
\(8\)\(3\)\(9\)

The signed deviations add to zero, but their squares add to \(18\). Both records equal to \(5\) remain in the count.

examples.title: Compare observed spread in context
examples.question:
Two observed batches contain lengths intended to be \(11\,\mathrm{cm}\):

\[\mathrm{A}:9,10,11,12,13,\qquad \mathrm{B}:3,9,11,15,17.\]

Compare their mean lengths and standard deviations, and say what the comparison shows about these recorded batches.
solution:
\[\mu_A=\frac{55}{5}=11\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\mu_B=\frac{55}{5}=11\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The means alone do not distinguish their variation.

Both recorded batch means equal the target. A has the smaller SD, so its observed lengths are more tightly grouped around that target. These small batches alone do not establish that future batches from A will always be more consistent.

examples.title: Use totals without reconstructing every record
examples.question: Eight masses, in grams, have total \(T=80\,\mathrm{g}\) and sum of squares \(Q=864\,\mathrm{g}^2\). Find the mean, centred sum of squares, descriptive variance and SD.
solution:
The equivalent direct formula gives the same result:

\[\sigma^2=\frac{864}{8}-\left(\frac{80}{8}\right)^2=108-100=8\,\mathrm{g}^2.\]

examples.title: The best reference leaves the original spread
examples.question: The fixed observations are \(2,5,5,8\). Compare their sum of squared distances from \(a=2\) with the smallest possible sum over all real reference values \(a\). State the original descriptive variance.
solution:
The actual mean is \(5\), and its centred sum of squares is

\[D=(2-5)^2+(5-5)^2+(5-5)^2+(8-5)^2=18.\]

\[S(2)=18+4(2-5)^2=54.\]

Directly, the squared distances are \(0,9,9,36\), which also total \(54\).

The square term is non-negative, so \(S(a)\) has minimum \(18\), only at \(a=5\). The variance of the original observations is always

\[\sigma^2=\frac{18}{4}=\frac{9}{2}.\]
The value \(\frac{S(2)}{4}=\frac{27}{2}\) is an average squared distance from the reference \(2\), not the original variance. Choosing the best reference does not turn the remaining spread into zero.

extraPractice.title: Square the deviations before averaging
extraPractice.prompt: Five lengths, in centimetres, are \(3,5,5,7,10\). Find the mean, the sum of signed deviations from that mean, the descriptive variance and the standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: Find the mean first. Positive and negative deviations cancel, so variance averages their squares rather than their signed values.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}=\frac{3+5+5+7+10}{5}=6\ \text{cm}.\]

  2. The signed deviations are \(-3,-1,-1,1,4\) cm. Their sum is \(0\) cm.

  3. \[\sum(x-\bar{x})^2=9+1+1+1+16=28\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]
  4. \[V=\frac{28}{5}\ \text{cm}^{2},\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{28}{5}}=\frac{2\sqrt{35}}{5}\ \text{cm}.\]

  5. A zero sum of signed deviations is expected at the mean. It does not imply zero spread.

extraPractice.title: Use both halves of an even-sized list
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered observations are \(2,3,4,5,5,8,10,12,13,25\). Use medians of the lower and upper halves for quartiles, retaining all ten observations. Find \(Q_1\), the median, \(Q_3\), IQR and range. Then replace only \(25\) by \(100\). Find the new range and decide how the IQR changes.

options.unknown: It cannot be calculated from the updated list.

extraPractice.hint: An even list splits into two equal halves without deleting either middle observation. The two halves here each have five values.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The lower half is \(2,3,4,5,5\), so \(Q_1=4\). The upper half is \(8,10,12,13,25\), so \(Q_3=12\).

  2. \[\text{median}=\frac{5+8}{2}=\frac{13}{2},\qquad \mathrm{IQR}=12-4=8.\]
  3. \[\text{range}=25-2=23,\qquad \text{new range}=100-2=98.\]

  4. The replacement remains the largest value. It changes neither half-median, so the IQR stays \(8\). This is a fact about this ordered list, not a claim that every change leaves the IQR fixed.

extraPractice.title: Exclude one middle position, not every equal value
extraPractice.prompt: The ordered observations are \(4,6,6,7,8,8,9,12,30\). Use medians of halves, excluding only the single overall middle observation because the count is odd. Find the median, both quartiles and the IQR.
extraPractice.hint: The fifth position is the overall median. The sixth observation is also \(8\), but it is a separate record and remains in the upper half.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The median is the fifth observation, \(8\). The lower half is \(4,6,6,7\), and the upper half is \(8,9,12,30\).

  2. \[Q_1=\frac{6+6}{2}=6,\qquad Q_3=\frac{9+12}{2}=\frac{21}{2}.\]
  3. \[\mathrm{IQR}=\frac{21}{2}-6=\frac{9}{2}.\]

  4. Deleting both observations equal to \(8\) would change the dataset and apply the stated rule incorrectly.

extraPractice.title: Recover a centred sum from moment totals
extraPractice.prompt: Eight measurements, in grams, have \(\sum x=96\) and \(\sum x^2=1248\). Find their mean, sum of squared deviations from the mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: The centred sum is \(\sum x^2-n\bar{x}^{\,2}\). It is a total; divide it by the number of observations to obtain variance.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}=\frac{96}{8}=12\ \text{g}.\]
  2. \[\sum(x-\bar{x})^2=1248-8(12^2)=96\ \text{g}^{2}.\]
  3. \[V=\frac{96}{8}=12\ \text{g}^{2},\qquad \sigma=2\sqrt{3}\ \text{g}.\]

  4. The totals are feasible; for example, \(8,8,8,12,12,16,16,16\) have these same count and moment totals.

extraPractice.title: Check whether the summary totals are possible
extraPractice.prompt: A report claims that six real observations have \(\sum x=42\) and \(\sum x^2=280\). Calculate the variance implied by these totals, the smallest possible sum of squares for six observations with total \(42\), and decide whether the report is consistent.

options.no: No: they imply a negative variance.
options.yes: Yes: the observations may include negative values.
options.round: Yes: take the absolute value of the variance.

extraPractice.hint: Every squared deviation is non-negative. A fixed total has its smallest sum of squares when all values equal their common mean.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}=\frac{42}{6}=7,\qquad V=\frac{280}{6}-7^2=-\frac{7}{3}.\]
  2. \[\sum x^2=\sum(x-7)^2+6(7^2)\ge294.\]

  3. The minimum \(294\) occurs for six copies of \(7\). The reported \(280\) is below this minimum, so no real dataset can satisfy the claim. Negative observations do not allow a negative variance.

starters.title: An unchanged IQR can hide wider extremes
starters.question:
Two machines aim to produce lengths of \(11\) cm. Seven observed lengths from each machine are:

A: \(8,9,10,11,12,13,14\).
B: \(2,9,10,11,12,13,20\).

Use medians of halves, excluding the single overall median in each odd-sized list. Show that the means are equal and calculate their common IQR. Calculate both descriptive variances. Which observed batch is more consistent around the target, and what does the equal IQR fail to show here?
starters.hint: Compare each observation with the common mean \(11\). The quartiles use the central values within each half, while variance uses all seven squared deviations.
starters.solution:
1. \[T_A=T_B=77,\qquad \bar{x}_A=\bar{x}_B=11\ \text{cm}.\]

  2. Each lower half has median \(9\), and each upper half has median \(13\). Both IQRs are \(13-9=4\) cm.

  3. \[V_A=\frac{9+4+1+0+1+4+9}{7}=4\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]
  4. \[V_B=\frac{81+4+1+0+1+4+81}{7}=\frac{172}{7}\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]

  5. Batch A has smaller variance about the same target. Its range is \(6\) cm, compared with \(18\) cm for B. The equal IQRs describe the same middle-half span but do not describe the different extremes.

  6. This comparison concerns the observed batches. It does not guarantee how every future item from either machine will behave.

• 1 mark: calculate the common mean from both totals.
  • 1 mark: apply the stated quartile convention and obtain the common IQR.
  • 1 mark: calculate A’s sum of squared deviations.
  • 1 mark: obtain A’s descriptive variance.
  • 1 mark: calculate B’s descriptive variance.
  • 1 mark: compare the observed batches in the target-length context.
  • 1 mark: explain what the IQR does not show and limit the conclusion to the observed data.

starters.title: The best reference does not remove the data spread
starters.question: For the fixed numerical observations \(2,6,9,11\), define \(F(a)=\sum(x-a)^2\), where \(a\) is any real reference value. Find the value of \(a\) that minimises \(F(a)\), the minimum sum, and the descriptive variance of the observations. Find every real \(a\) such that \(F(a)=82\). Explain why the minimum sum is positive.
starters.hint: Find the actual mean and the centred sum of squares. Write \(F(a)\) as that minimum plus a non-negative square.
starters.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}=\frac{2+6+9+11}{4}=7,\qquad Q=4+36+81+121=242.\]
  2. \[\sum(x-7)^2=242-4(7^2)=46.\]
  3. \[F(a)=46+4(a-7)^2.\]

  4. The non-negative square vanishes only at \(a=7\). The minimum sum is \(46\), and the descriptive variance is \(\frac{46}{4}=\frac{23}{2}\).

  5. \[F(a)=82\Longleftrightarrow4(a-7)^2=36\Longleftrightarrow a-7=\pm3.\]
  6. \[a=4\quad\text{or}\quad a=10.\]

  7. The fixed observations are unequal, so no single reference can make every squared distance zero. Moving the reference changes \(F(a)\); it does not change the data’s actual mean or variance.

  • 1 mark: calculate the centred sum.

  • 1 mark: state the minimum sum and its reference value.
  • 1 mark: distinguish the minimum total from descriptive variance.
  • 1 mark: find both reference values satisfying the target.

revision.body:
Use centre and spread together. Keep quartile positions and squared deviations distinct.

Range and quartiles describe different spans

\[\text{range}=x_{\max}-x_{\min},\qquad \mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1.\]

Order all records and retain repeats. Quartiles are medians of the two halves. For odd \(n\), exclude only the single overall middle record. For even \(n\), keep all records in equal halves. Follow any different rule in the question.

Range uses extremes. An extreme can move while the quartiles and IQR stay fixed.

Variance averages squared deviations

\[V=\frac{\sum(x-\bar{x})^2}{n},\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{V},\qquad n>0.\]

Use the full count \(n\) for these descriptive summaries. Variance has squared units; SD uses the original units. Signed deviations sum to zero at the mean, even when spread is positive. Variance and SD are zero exactly when every observation is equal.

Moment totals give the same spread

\[T=\sum x,\quad Q=\sum x^2,\quad \bar{x}=\frac{T}{n},\quad V=\frac{Q}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]\[\sum(x-\bar{x})^2=Q-\frac{T^2}{n}\ge0.\]

The centred sum is a total: divide by \(n\) before taking the square root for SD. Do not confuse \(\sum x^2\) with \((\sum x)^2\). An exact negative variance means an arithmetic error or inconsistent information. Keep full precision until the final answer.

The mean minimises squared distance

\[\sum(x-a)^2=nV+n(a-\bar{x})^2.\]

The minimum total is \(nV\), only at \(a=\bar{x}\), and is positive for unequal observations. Moving the reference leaves the data and variance fixed. Averaging squared distances about any other reference does not give variance.

Compare centre and spread with units and context. Equal means or equal IQRs do not prove identical distributions. Limit conclusions to the evidence supplied.
revision.checks:
• Quartile rule stated and every repeated record retained?
  • Centred sum distinguished from variance and SD?
  • Divisor, units and non-negative square root correct?
  • Comparison supported by both figures and context?

orig_9709_s1_var_coded_totals.description: Keep the direction of a code clear. Restore the original mean and spread, move between origins, and recover complete moment totals before solving reverse calibration problems.

sections.title: How do translated totals give the original spread?
sections.label: Translation totals
sections.intro:
Coding writes every original observation on a simpler scale. For a translation \(u=x-c\), define \(S_u=\sum u\), \(Q_u=\sum u^2\), and use the positive count \(n\):

\[\bar{u}=\frac{S_u}{n},\qquad\sigma_u^2=\frac{Q_u}{n}-\left(\frac{S_u}{n}\right)^2.\]

These are descriptive summaries, using divisor \(n\). The inverse rule is \(x=c+u\), so

\[\bar{x}=c+\bar{u},\qquad\sigma_x^2=\sigma_u^2,\qquad\sigma_x=\sigma_u.\]

blocks.html: A convenient origin \(c\) is not necessarily the true mean. Do not assume \(S_u=0\) or omit the coded-mean square. Exact coded variance must be non-negative.

blocks.title: A chosen origin need not be the mean
blocks.prompt: Five masses \(x\), in grams, are coded by \(u=x-60\). Their coded totals are \(\sum u=-10\) and \(\sum u^2=50\). Find the original mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation.
blocks.hint: The coded mean is not zero. Subtract its square when calculating variance; translation then changes the mean but leaves spread unchanged.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\bar{u}=\frac{-10}{5}=-2,\qquad\sigma_u^2=\frac{50}{5}-(-2)^2=6.\]
  2. \[\bar{x}=60-2=58\,\mathrm{g},\qquad\sigma_x^2=6\,\mathrm{g}^2,\qquad\sigma_x=\sqrt{6}\,\mathrm{g}.\]

sections.title: What changes under a scale or sign reversal?
sections.label: Scale and order
sections.intro:
For \(u=\frac{x-a}{b}\), require \(b\ne0\) and first write the inverse \(x=a+bu\). Then

\[\bar{x}=a+b\bar{u},\qquad\sigma_x^2=b^2\sigma_u^2,\qquad\sigma_x=|b|\sigma_u,\]\[\text{range}_x=|b|\text{range}_u,\qquad\mathrm{IQR}_x=|b|\mathrm{IQR}_u.\]

The mean uses the signed scale. Spread measures use its magnitude, or its square for variance. With \(b>0\), order is preserved. With \(b<0\), order reverses and the lower and upper quartiles swap roles:

\[Q_{1,x}=a+bQ_{3,u},\qquad Q_{3,x}=a+bQ_{1,u}\qquad(b<0).\]

Use the same stated quartile convention on both scales. Translation alone leaves range and IQR unchanged as well as variance and SD.

blocks.title: A negative scale reverses positions, not spread signs
blocks.prompt: Four numerical lengths \(x\), in centimetres, are coded by \(u=\frac{x-18}{-3}\). The ordered coded observations are \(-1,3,3,3\). Find the original mean, descriptive variance, SD, range and IQR. For quartiles, use medians of the lower and upper halves, retaining all four records.
blocks.hint: Reverse the code to \(x=18-3u\). Use the signed scale for the mean, its square for variance and its absolute value for range and IQR.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\bar{u}=\frac{-1+3+3+3}{4}=2,\qquad\sigma_u^2=\frac{1+9+9+9}{4}-2^2=3.\]
  2. \[\bar{x}=18-3(2)=12\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\sigma_x^2=(-3)^2(3)=27\,\mathrm{cm}^2,\qquad\sigma_x=3\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  3. The coded range is \(3-(-1)=4\). The two half-medians are \(Q_{1,u}=1\) and \(Q_{3,u}=3\), giving coded IQR \(2\).

    \[\text{range}_x=3(4)=12\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\mathrm{IQR}_x=3(2)=6\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  4. The reversed original order is \(9,9,9,21\). Its quartiles are \(9\) and \(15\), confirming IQR \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\). Both repeated observations and their positions matter.

sections.title: How do I move from one origin to another?
sections.label: Two origins
sections.intro:
Write \(D_c=\sum(x-c)\) and \(E_c=\sum(x-c)^2\). If the new origin is \(d\), let \(h=d-c\). Since \(x-d=(x-c)-h\),

\[D_d=D_c-nh,\qquad E_d=E_c-2hD_c+nh^2.\]

The coded sums change, but the original mean and variance agree:

\[\bar{x}=c+\frac{D_c}{n}=d+\frac{D_d}{n},\]\[\sigma_x^2=\frac{E_c}{n}-\left(\frac{D_c}{n}\right)^2=\frac{E_d}{n}-\left(\frac{D_d}{n}\right)^2.\]

blocks.html:
Keep the sign of \(h=d-c\), including when the origin moves down. For distinct origins, the two first totals can recover the count:

\[n=\frac{D_c-D_d}{d-c}.\]

Check that it is a positive integer. Identical origins give no new count equation when the totals agree, and inconsistent totals when they disagree.

blocks.title: Move the origin backwards
blocks.prompt:
The same numerical observations satisfy

\[\sum(x-14)=6,\qquad\sum(x-14)^2=46,\qquad\sum(x-10)=30.\]

Find their count, the sum of squares about origin \(10\), the original mean and descriptive variance.
blocks.hint: The change of origin is \(h=10-14=-4\). Keep that sign in both the linear and squared-total updates.
blocks.solution:
1. \[30=6-n(-4)\Longrightarrow n=6.\]
  2. \[\sum(x-10)^2=46-2(-4)(6)+6(-4)^2=190.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}=10+\frac{30}{6}=15.\]
  4. \[\sigma^2=\frac{190}{6}-\left(\frac{30}{6}\right)^2=\frac{20}{3}.\]

    The original origin gives the same value: \(\frac{46}{6}-1^2=\frac{20}{3}\).

sections.title: How do I restore the original total and sum of squares?
sections.label: Recover raw moments
sections.intro:
From \(x=a+bu\), sum the expression and its full square:

\[T=\sum x=na+bS_u,\]\[Q=\sum x^2=na^2+2abS_u+b^2Q_u.\]

The middle term comes from the product of the shift and coded part. After restoring \(T\) and \(Q\), use

\[\bar{x}=\frac{T}{n},\qquad\sum(x-\bar{x})^2=Q-\frac{T^2}{n},\qquad\sigma_x^2=\frac{Q}{n}-\bar{x}^{\,2}.\]

blocks.html:
\[\sum x=6(40)+2(6)=252,\qquad\bar x=\frac{252}{6}=42.\]\[\sum x^2=na^2+2ab\sum u+b^2\sum u^2.\]
TermWorkingValue
Origin\(6(40)^2\)9600
Cross term\(2(40)(2)(6)\)960
Scaled squares\(2^2(24)\)96
\[\sigma_x^2=\frac{10656}{6}-42^2=12.\]

With origin \(44\) and scale \(2\), the new code sums are \(\sum v=-6\) and \(\sum v^2=24\). The same total is \(11616-1056+96=10656\). The cross term can be negative.

For \(a=40\), \(b=2\), \(n=6\), \(S_u=6\), \(Q_u=24\), the three contributions are \(9600+960+96=10656\).

blocks.title: Restore the cross term
blocks.prompt: Three numerical observations are coded by \(u=\frac{x-8}{-2}\), with \(\sum u=-3\) and \(\sum u^2=9\). Find the original total, original sum of squares and descriptive variance.
blocks.hint: Write \(x=8-2u\), then expand its square before summing. The product of the negative scale and negative coded total gives a positive cross term here.

blocks.html: For two groups with different codes, restore each group’s count, original total and sum of squares separately. Convert them to one common measurement unit, then combine those quantities. Coded totals from different origins or scales cannot be pooled directly.

sections.title: Can mean and SD identify a calibration?
sections.label: Calibration cases
sections.intro:
For a forward rule \(y=px+q\), use

\[\bar{y}=p\bar{x}+q,\qquad\sigma_y=|p|\sigma_x.\]

If both SDs are positive, find \(|p|=\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}\), retain both possible signs, then calculate \(q=\bar{y}-p\bar{x}\) for each. Keep each scale paired with its own shift, and apply any stated order restriction.

blocks.html:
Zero spread must be checked without dividing by it:

Input SDTarget SDForward-rule conclusion
\(\sigma_x>0\)\(\sigma_y=0\)\(p=0\), with \(q=\bar{y}\). Possible only if a constant forward rule is allowed.
\(\sigma_x=0\)\(\sigma_y>0\)Impossible: equal inputs cannot produce unequal outputs under one fixed rule.
\(\sigma_x=0\)\(\sigma_y=0\)The mean condition \(q=\bar{y}-p\bar{x}\) remains. It does not identify a unique scale.

A forward rule may allow \(p=0\), producing constant outputs. Invertible coding requires a nonzero scale; it cannot restore original inputs after all values have collapsed to one output. In the last table row, retain only nonzero scales if invertibility is required.

blocks.title: Do not divide by a zero standard deviation
blocks.prompt: A forward calibration \(y=px+q\) is allowed to use \(p=0\). First, every input equals \(4\), and the required outputs must all equal \(13\). Which family of rules works? Separately, inputs have mean \(4\) and positive SD \(2\), and the target output has mean \(13\) and SD \(0\). Find \((p,q)\) for that second case and decide whether it is invertible.

fields.label: All rules for the constant-input case

options.impossible: No rule exists because the input SD is zero.

options.no: No: every input is mapped to the same output.
options.yes: Yes: all linear forward rules are invertible.

blocks.hint: Use \(\sigma_y=|p|\sigma_x\) directly. When both SDs are zero, the mean equation remains but the SD equation may give no restriction on the scale.
blocks.solution:
1. For the constant input \(x=4\), the required output gives \(4p+q=13\), so

    \[q=13-4p,\qquad p\in\mathbb{R}.\]

    Every such rule sends all inputs to \(13\).

  2. For the separate nonconstant input,

    \[0=|p|(2)\Longrightarrow p=0,\qquad13=0(4)+q\Longrightarrow q=13.\]

  3. The rule \(y=13\) loses all distinctions between inputs, so it has no inverse. It is a valid allowed forward calibration but cannot be used as reversible coding.

glossary.definition: The chosen value subtracted from each original observation; it need not be the actual mean.
The sum \(S_u=\sum u\) of all coded observations.
The sum \(Q_u=\sum u^2\), formed by squaring each code before adding.
The equation restoring each original observation from its code, with a nonzero scale.
A multiplier whose sign controls direction and whose magnitude controls distances.
The change that sends larger coded values to smaller original values under a negative inverse scale.
The contribution \(2abS_u\) in the original sum of squares when \(x=a+bu\).
Replacing origin \(c\) by \(d\), with signed shift \(h=d-c\).
A forward rule \(y=px+q\) designed to produce required summaries.
All records have the same value. It must be handled directly rather than by dividing by their SD.

examples.title: Translate the origin and retain the coded mean
examples.question: The six numerical observations are \(36,40,42,42,46,46\). Code them using \(u=x-40\), then use the coded totals to find their original mean, descriptive variance and SD.
solution: The chosen origin is \(40\), while the actual mean is \(42\). Subtracting the origin did not make the coded mean zero.

examples.title: Decode positive and negative scales
examples.question: The six coded observations \(u\) are \(-2,0,1,1,3,3\), with \(x=40+2u\). Find the original mean, variance, range and IQR. Use median-of-halves quartiles, retaining all six observations in two equal halves. Then check the quartiles using the alternative code \(v=-u\), so \(x=40-2v\).
solution:
The coded range is \(3-(-2)=5\). The halves \((-2,0,1)\) and \((1,3,3)\) have medians \(0\) and \(3\), so their IQR is \(3\).

\[\text{range}_x=2(5)=10,\qquad\mathrm{IQR}_x=2(3)=6.\]

The negative code in increasing order is

\[v:\ -3,-3,-1,-1,0,2.\]

Its half-medians are \(Q_{1,v}=-3\) and \(Q_{3,v}=0\). Because \(x=40-2v\) reverses order,

\[Q_{1,x}=40-2Q_{3,v}=40,\qquad Q_{3,x}=40-2Q_{1,v}=46.\]
The original IQR is again \(46-40=6\). This code has mean \(-1\) and variance \(3\), which restore original mean \(42\) and variance \(12\) through the same inverse rule.

examples.title: Recover the count while changing origins
examples.question:
The same numerical dataset has unknown positive integer count \(n\) and satisfies

\[D_{25}=\sum(x-25)=15,\qquad E_{25}=\sum(x-25)^2=65,\qquad D_{29}=-5.\]

Find \(n\), \(E_{29}\), the original mean and descriptive variance.
solution:
The new origin is four greater, so each coded value falls by \(4\):

\[-5=15-4n\Longrightarrow n=5.\]

The first origin confirms the result:

\[25+\frac{15}{5}=28,\qquad\frac{65}{5}-\left(\frac{15}{5}\right)^2=4.\]

The count is a positive integer, and both origins describe the same original summaries.

examples.title: Reconstruct all three parts of the raw square
examples.question: For six numerical observations, \(u=\frac{x-40}{2}\), \(S_u=6\) and \(Q_u=24\). Recover the original total \(T\), sum of squares \(Q\), centred sum of squares and descriptive variance.
solution: The cross term \(960\) is essential. It disappears only when its factors make it zero; it is not optional because the calculation uses coded data.

examples.title: Retain both possible calibration signs
examples.question: Input observations have mean \(8\) and SD \(3\). A calibration \(y=px+q\) must give mean \(20\) and SD \(6\). Find all parameter pairs \((p,q)\), then select the pair that preserves the order of unequal inputs.
solution: Both produce the required mean and SD. Preserving the order of unequal inputs requires \(p>0\), so it selects \((2,4)\). The negative choice reverses that order.

related.title: Coded data, scale changes and unknown observations

extraPractice.title: A convenient origin need not be the mean
extraPractice.prompt: Eight lengths \(x\), in centimetres, are coded by \(u=x-250\). Their coded totals are \(\sum u=-12\) and \(\sum u^2=60\). Find the original mean, descriptive variance and standard deviation.
extraPractice.hint: The coded mean is negative, not zero. Translation restores the mean but leaves variance and SD unchanged.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{u}=-\frac{12}{8}=-\frac{3}{2},\qquad \bar{x}=250-\frac{3}{2}=\frac{497}{2}\ \text{cm}.\]
  2. \[V_u=\frac{60}{8}-\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)^2=\frac{21}{4}.\]
  3. \[V_x=\frac{21}{4}\ \text{cm}^{2},\qquad \sigma_x=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2}\ \text{cm}.\]

  4. The negative coded total places the mean below the chosen origin. It does not indicate negative spread.

extraPractice.title: Undo a negative scale for every spread measure
extraPractice.prompt: Lengths \(x\), in centimetres, are coded by \(u=\frac{60-x}{3}\). For five coded records, \(\sum u=10\), \(\sum u^2=30\), the coded range is \(4\), and the coded IQR is \(3\). Find the original mean, descriptive variance, SD, range and IQR.
extraPractice.hint: Write the inverse first: \(x=60-3u\). Use the signed multiplier for the mean, its square for variance, and its absolute value for SD, range and IQR.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{u}=\frac{10}{5}=2,\qquad V_u=\frac{30}{5}-2^2=2.\]
  2. \[\bar{x}=60-3(2)=54\ \text{cm},\qquad V_x=(-3)^2(2)=18\ \text{cm}^{2}.\]
  3. \[\sigma_x=3\sqrt{2}\ \text{cm},\qquad R_x=3(4)=12\ \text{cm},\qquad \mathrm{IQR}_x=3(3)=9\ \text{cm}.\]

  4. The negative multiplier reverses order. Lower and upper quartiles swap their roles under the transformation, leaving the IQR positive.

extraPractice.title: Move to a lower reference value
extraPractice.prompt: For six numerical observations, \(D_{40}=\sum(x-40)=-12\) and \(E_{40}=\sum(x-40)^2=54\). Find \(D_{35}\), \(E_{35}\), the original mean and the descriptive variance. Explain why changing the reference does not change the variance.

fields.label: Sum of squares about the new reference

extraPractice.hint: Use \(h=35-40=-5\). Retain the signs in both \(D_{35}=D_{40}-nh\) and the cross term in the new sum of squares.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[h=-5,\qquad D_{35}=-12-6(-5)=18.\]
  2. \[E_{35}=54-2(-5)(-12)+6(-5)^2=54-120+150=84.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}=35+\frac{18}{6}=38,\qquad V=\frac{84}{6}-\left(\frac{18}{6}\right)^2=5.\]

  4. The old origin confirms the same variance:

    \[V=\frac{54}{6}-\left(-\frac{12}{6}\right)^2=5.\]

  5. The coded totals change, but the original observations and their distances from their actual mean do not.

extraPractice.title: Keep the signed cross term
extraPractice.prompt: Four masses \(x\), in grams, are coded by \(u=\frac{x-15}{-2}\). The coded totals are \(\sum u=-2\) and \(\sum u^2=14\). Recover \(\sum x\), \(\sum x^2\), the original mean and the descriptive variance.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(x=15-2u\). Expand each square before summing: \(x^2=225-60u+4u^2\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sum x=4(15)-2(-2)=64\ \text{g}.\]
  2. \[\sum x^2=4(225)-60(-2)+4(14)=900+120+56=1076\ \text{g}^{2}.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}=\frac{64}{4}=16\ \text{g},\qquad V_x=\frac{1076}{4}-16^2=13\ \text{g}^{2}.\]

  4. Checking through the coded variance gives

    \[V_u=\frac{14}{4}-\left(-\frac{2}{4}\right)^2=\frac{13}{4},\qquad V_x=4V_u=13.\]

  5. The cross term is positive here because both its coefficient and the coded total are negative.

extraPractice.title: Recover a count and verify the second origin
extraPractice.prompt: The same numerical observations have \(D_{12}=24\), \(D_{16}=-8\) and \(E_{12}=104\), where \(D_c=\sum(x-c)\) and \(E_c=\sum(x-c)^2\). Find the count, original mean, descriptive variance and \(E_{16}\). Separately, could \(D_{12}=24\) and \(D_{16}=-10\) describe any finite dataset?

fields.label: Is the separate count proposal feasible?

options.no: No: it requires a non-integer count.
options.yes: Yes: the observations themselves may be non-integers.

extraPractice.hint: The difference between two first totals equals the number of observations times the difference between their origins. The count must be a positive integer even when the data values are real.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[D_{12}-D_{16}=n(16-12)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad24-(-8)=4n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=8.\]
  2. \[\bar{x}=12+\frac{24}{8}=15,\qquad V=\frac{104}{8}-\left(\frac{24}{8}\right)^2=4.\]
  3. \[E_{16}=104-2(4)(24)+8(4^2)=40.\]
  4. \[\frac{E_{16}}{8}-\left(\frac{D_{16}}{8}\right)^2=\frac{40}{8}-(-1)^2=4.\]

  5. For the separate proposal,

    \[24-(-10)=4n\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=\frac{17}{2}.\]

  6. This is not an integer, so no dataset with a finite number of records can satisfy the two stated totals.

starters.title: Retain both calibrations before using the ordering
starters.question: The numerical observations \(3,3,11,11\) are transformed by \(y=px+q\), where \(p,q\) are real constants. The transformed mean is \(10\) and its descriptive SD is \(6\). Find every ordered pair \((p,q)\). Additional information says that the larger original observations become the smaller transformed observations. Select the pair satisfying this condition, then find the transformed range and IQR, using medians of halves for the quartiles.
starters.hint: Find the original mean and SD. SD determines the magnitude of \(p\), while the mean determines \(q\) for each sign. Reversed order selects the negative multiplier.
starters.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}=\frac{3+3+11+11}{4}=7,\qquad V_x=\frac{16+16+16+16}{4}=16,\qquad \sigma_x=4.\]
  2. \[6=|p|(4)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=\pm\frac{3}{2}.\]
  3. \[q=10-7p.\]

    For \(p=\frac{3}{2}\), \(q=-\frac{1}{2}\); for \(p=-\frac{3}{2}\), \(q=\frac{41}{2}\). Both give the required mean and SD.

  4. Reversed order requires \(p\lt0\), selecting

    \[(p,q)=\left(-\frac{3}{2},\frac{41}{2}\right).\]

  5. The original lower and upper quartiles are \(3\) and \(11\), so both original range and IQR equal \(8\). Therefore

    \[R_y=\frac{3}{2}(8)=12,\qquad \mathrm{IQR}_y=\frac{3}{2}(8)=12.\]

  6. Direct substitution gives transformed records \(16,16,4,4\). Their ordered form \(4,4,16,16\) has mean \(10\), SD \(6\), range \(12\) and IQR \(12\), confirming all conditions.

• 1 mark: calculate the original mean and SD.
  • 1 mark: obtain both possible signs of the scale factor.
  • 1 mark: recover the matching shift for each sign.
  • 1 mark: verify both unrestricted calibration pairs.
  • 1 mark: use reversed order to select the negative scale.
  • 1 mark: calculate the transformed range.
  • 1 mark: calculate the transformed IQR with the stated quartile convention.

starters.title: Check zero spread before dividing
starters.question: In this question \(y=px+q\) is a forward transformation and \(p=0\) is allowed. First, the original list is \(5,5,5,5,5\). Describe all choices of \(p,q\) giving transformed mean \(11\) and SD \(0\). Could this same constant list instead be transformed to SD \(3\)? In a separate case, the original list is \(3,7\): find \(p,q\) giving transformed mean \(11\) and SD \(0\), and decide whether this last transformation has an inverse on the two original values.
starters.hint: Use \(V_y=p^2V_x\), which also holds for zero variance and zero multipliers. Do not divide by a zero original SD.
starters.solution:
1. For five copies of \(5\), every transformed observation is \(5p+q\). Its SD is zero for every real \(p,q\). To obtain mean \(11\),

    \[5p+q=11\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=11-5p.\]

  2. There are infinitely many such pairs. No transformation of this form can give positive SD to the constant list, because the outputs remain equal.

  3. For the separate list \(3,7\), the mean is \(5\) and variance is \(4\). Thus

    \[V_y=4p^2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=0.\]
  4. \[\bar{y}=5(0)+q=11\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=11.\]

  5. The output list is \(11,11\), so the requested mean and SD are correct. Both distinct inputs have the same output, and an inverse cannot recover which input was used.

  6. This forward transformation is permitted by the question. It would not be allowed as an invertible code requiring a nonzero scale.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: recognise that the constant original list stays constant.
  • 1 mark: derive the complete family of shifts and scales.
  • 1 mark: reject the positive-SD target for constant input.
  • 1 mark: use positive original variance to force a zero multiplier in the separate case.
  • 1 mark: obtain and verify the required shift.
  • 1 mark: explain the loss of an inverse and distinguish it from invertible coding.

revision.body:
Write the inverse, keep signs in the mean, and use squared or absolute scales for spread.

Decode the mean and spread

\[u=\frac{x-a}{b}\ \Longrightarrow\ x=a+bu,\qquad b\ne0.\]

With \(S=\sum u\), \(R=\sum u^2\) and count \(n>0\),

\[\bar{u}=\frac{S}{n},\qquad V_u=\frac{R}{n}-\bar{u}^{\,2}.\]\[\bar{x}=a+b\bar{u},\qquad V_x=b^2V_u,\qquad \sigma_x=|b|\sigma_u.\]

Range and IQR also scale by \(|b|\). A negative multiplier reverses order; it does not give negative spread.

Restore the original moment totals

\[\sum x=na+bS,\qquad \sum x^2=na^2+2abS+b^2R.\]

Keep the signed cross term \(2abS\). Square each coded value before summing; \(R\) is not \(S^2\). Original and coded moments must use consistent counts and units.

Move between two origins

Let \(D_c=\sum(x-c)\), \(E_c=\sum(x-c)^2\), and \(h=d-c\). Then

\[D_d=D_c-nh,\qquad E_d=E_c-2hD_c+nh^2.\]

For distinct origins, an unknown count is

\[n=\frac{D_c-D_d}{d-c}.\]

Check that \(n\) is a positive integer. Both origins describe the same original mean and variance, although the coded totals change.

Keep every valid calibration

For \(y=px+q\) with \(\sigma_x>0\),

\[|p|=\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x},\qquad q=\bar{y}-p\bar{x}.\]

Retain both signs when the target SD is positive, then use any ordering condition. A zero target SD forces \(p=0\). Constant input (\(\sigma_x=0\)) stays constant under every such rule: a positive target SD is impossible, and the mean alone fixes a relation between \(p,q\). A zero scale has no inverse.
revision.checks:
• Inverse direction, count and signed cross term correct?
  • Coded quantities distinguished from original units and moments?
  • Both scale signs and zero-spread exceptions considered?

orig_9709_s1_var_reconstruction.description: Work backwards from totals and variance to recover every possible count, mean or coding origin. Then check whether actual observations can satisfy the summaries and the stated restrictions.

sections.title: Could these summaries come from real observations?
sections.label: Feasible moments
sections.intro:
Write \(n\) for a positive integer count, \(T=\sum x\), \(Q=\sum x^2\), mean \(\mu=\frac{T}{n}\), and descriptive variance

\[V=\frac{Q}{n}-\left(\frac{T}{n}\right)^2.\]

The centred sum of squares is \(D=Q-\frac{T^2}{n}\), so real observations require

\[Q\ge\frac{T^2}{n}.\]

Equality means every record equals \(\mu\), giving zero variance. If \(n=1\), equality is compulsory: the single record is \(T\), so \(Q=T^2\) and \(V=0\).

blocks.html: For \(n\ge2\) with unrestricted real observations, the bound is also sufficient. Put \(d=\sqrt{\frac{D}{2}}\). The list containing \(\mu-d,\mu+d\) and \(n-2\) copies of \(\mu\) has exactly total \(T\) and sum of squares \(Q\). This proves existence of real records, without proving they are integers or non-negative.

\[Q-\frac{T^2}{n}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\ge0.\]
PointSum of squaresAt total 6
A14Possible, e.g. 1, 2, 3
B12Possible, all records equal 2
C10Impossible

For \(n\ge2\) and \(Q\ge\frac{T^2}{n}\), one construction is \(\mu-d,\ \mu+d\) and \(n-2\) copies of \(\mu=\frac{T}{n}\), where \(d=\sqrt{\frac{Q-\tfrac{T^2}{n}}{2}}\). For one record, equality \(Q=T^2\) is required.

Extra restrictions such as integers or nonnegative observations require a separate check.

With \(n=3\) and \(T=6\), the boundary is \(Q=12\). Below it no real records exist; at it all records equal \(2\); above it real constructions are possible.

blocks.title: Find the least possible sum of squares
blocks.prompt: Four unrestricted real observations have total \(T=8\). Find the least possible sum of squares \(Q\), and identify the observations at equality. For a separate dataset with this same count and total but \(Q=24\), find the descriptive variance.

options.distinct: Any four distinct values with total eight.

blocks.hint: The squared-deviation total is \(Q-\frac{T^2}{n}\). Its minimum is zero, attained only when all records equal the mean.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu=\frac{8}{4}=2,\qquad Q\ge\frac{8^2}{4}=16.\]

  2. Equality requires all four observations to be \(2\), giving sum of squares \(4(2^2)=16\).

  3. \[V=\frac{24}{4}-2^2=2.\]

    For example, \(0,2,2,4\) has the required count, total and sum of squares.

sections.title: How do I recover every possible count?
sections.label: Unknown counts
sections.intro:
If \(T,Q,V\) are known but \(n\) is not, start from the descriptive variance equation. Multiplying by \(n^2\) gives

\[Vn^2-Qn+T^2=0.\]

Solve for every algebraic value, then keep only positive integers. Check each retained count in the original formula and the real-data conditions. In particular, a count of one must give zero variance and \(Q=T^2\), even if it satisfies the rearranged equation.

blocks.html: A quadratic can give two valid counts. Do not choose one just because it is smaller or looks more likely. A zero, negative or non-integer root is not a number of records.

\[\frac{60}{n}-\left(\frac{12}{n}\right)^2=6\quad\Rightarrow\quad(n-4)(n-6)=0.\]
CountMeanVarianceExample records
43\(\frac{60}4-3^2=6\)1, 1, 3, 7
62\(\frac{60}6-2^2=6\)0, 0, 1, 1, 3, 7

Each example has total \(12\) and sum of squares \(60\). Both counts are positive integers and give feasible records.

For \(T=12\), \(Q=60\), \(V=6\), both \(n=4\) and \(n=6\) pass. Their means are \(3\) and \(2\), respectively.

If \(V=0\), the equation is no longer quadratic. For \(Q>0\), solve \(n=\frac{T^2}{Q}\) and enforce the count conditions; all records must then equal \(\frac{T}{n}\). If \(Q=0\), every real record must be zero: \(T=0\) allows any positive integer count, while \(T\ne0\) is impossible. Negative variance or a negative sum of squares is invalid from the start.

blocks.title: Reject a false singleton and handle zero variance
blocks.prompt: Unrestricted real observations have \(T=6\), \(Q=45\) and descriptive variance \(V=9\). Find all valid positive integer counts. Separately, a dataset has \(T=10\), \(Q=20\) and \(V=0\): find its count. Finally, which counts are possible when \(T=Q=V=0\)?

fields.label: All counts for the first dataset
Counts when all three summaries are zero

blocks.hint: Solving the count equation is only the first step. One observation must have zero variance and its sum of squares must equal the square of its total.
blocks.solution:
1. \[9n^2-45n+36=0\Longrightarrow(n-1)(n-4)=0.\]

  2. The algebra gives \(1\) and \(4\). A single observation with total \(6\) would have \(Q=36\) and variance zero, so \(n=1\) is invalid.

  3. \[n=4:\qquad \frac{45}{4}-\left(\frac{6}{4}\right)^2=9.\]

    This count is feasible for unrestricted real records, so the complete answer is \(\{4\}\).

  4. For the separate zero-variance dataset,

    \[-20n+100=0\Longrightarrow n=5.\]

    Five copies of \(2\) give its stated totals.

  5. If \(T=Q=V=0\), any positive number of zero observations works. The count is not uniquely determined.

sections.title: Why can an unknown mean have two signs?
sections.label: Mean branches
sections.intro:
Rearrange the variance formula to obtain

\[\mu^2=\frac{Q}{n}-V.\]

A positive right-hand side gives both square-root signs; zero gives the single mean \(0\); a negative value gives no real mean. Each branch has its own total \(T=n\mu\). Apply sign or context information only after identifying every branch.

blocks.title: Keep both mean signs until a condition selects one
blocks.prompt: Five unrestricted real observations have \(Q=100\) and descriptive variance \(16\). Find all possible means, then select the mean if the total is positive. Could a separate dataset instead have the same count and variance but \(Q=70\)?

fields.label: Mean when the total is positive

options.no: No: it would require a negative squared mean.
options.yes: Yes: choose the negative square root.
options.zero: Yes: its mean must be zero.

blocks.hint: Rearrange to \(\mu^2=\frac{Q}{n}-V\). A positive squared mean gives two signs; a negative squared mean gives no real value.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\mu^2=\frac{100}{5}-16=4\Longrightarrow\mu=-2\text{ or }\mu=2.\]

  2. The corresponding totals are \(-10\) and \(10\). A positive total selects \(\mu=2\).

  3. The separate proposal gives

    \[\mu^2=\frac{70}{5}-16=-2.\]

    No real mean has a negative square.

sections.title: How do I recover a hidden coding origin?
sections.label: Unknown origins
sections.intro:
For \(D_c=\sum(x-c)\) and \(E_c=\sum(x-c)^2\), the first moment gives

\[D_c=n(\mu-c),\qquad c=\mu-\frac{D_c}{n}.\]

The coded moments also determine the original variance:

\[V=\frac{E_c}{n}-\left(\frac{D_c}{n}\right)^2.\]

If \(\mu\) is unknown, use other supplied moments to recover all possible means first, then pair each one with its origin. Check the second moment as well:

\[Q=E_c+2cD_c+nc^2.\]

blocks.title: Check a hidden origin against both moments
blocks.prompt:
Four numerical observations have mean \(7\). Relative to an unknown origin \(c\),

\[D_c=\sum(x-c)=-8,\qquad E_c=\sum(x-c)^2=24.\]

Find \(c\), the descriptive variance and the original sum of squares.
blocks.hint: The first coded total identifies the origin. Use the second coded total to recover variance and then verify the raw sum of squares.
blocks.solution:
1. \[-8=4(7-c)\Longrightarrow c=9.\]
  2. \[V=\frac{24}{4}-\left(\frac{-8}{4}\right)^2=2.\]
  3. \[Q=4(2+7^2)=204.\]

  4. The full inverse expansion confirms it:

    \[E_c+2cD_c+nc^2=24+2(9)(-8)+4(9^2)=204.\]

blocks.html: An origin that fits the first total may still contradict the sum of squares or a separately supplied variance. Restore every original condition before accepting a pair. Keep a valid negative origin unless the question excludes it.

sections.title: What changes when observations must be counts or non-negative?
sections.label: Context restrictions
sections.intro:
The real-data bound does not by itself settle extra restrictions. Non-negative observations require \(T\ge0\) and \(Q\le T^2\): expanding the square of their total gives all their squares plus non-negative cross terms.

Integer observations must have integer totals and sums of squares, but those tests alone may still be insufficient. Solve for the values when possible, or list all small allowed combinations. Apply the actual restrictions to the observations, not just to the recovered mean or count.

blocks.title: Real observations need not be whole-number counts
blocks.prompt: Two observations have total \(7\) and sum of squares \(27\). Find both observation values, without assigning labels. Decide whether these summaries are possible for non-negative real observations and whether they are possible for non-negative integer counts.

options.realonly: Non-negative real observations are possible; non-negative integer counts are not.

blocks.hint: Find the product from the sum and sum of squares, then solve the quadratic. Check the actual values against each stated restriction.
blocks.solution:
1. \[ab=\frac{(a+b)^2-(a^2+b^2)}{2}=\frac{49-27}{2}=11.\]
  2. \[z^2-7z+11=0\Longrightarrow z=\frac{7\pm\sqrt{5}}{2}.\]

  3. Both roots are positive real numbers, and their sum and sum of squares are \(7\) and \(27\). They are not integers.

  4. Equivalently, the non-negative integer pairs with sum \(7\), up to order, are \((0,7),(1,6),(2,5),(3,4)\). Their sums of squares are \(49,37,29,25\); none is \(27\).

blocks.html: A constructed real example proves real feasibility. If that particular example contains a negative or non-integer value, it does not automatically rule out every alternative construction. Use a necessary bound, an exhaustive list or the complete set of solutions to justify impossibility under extra conditions.

glossary.definition: The original total \(T=\sum x\) and sum of squares \(Q=\sum x^2\), used with the record count to calculate mean and variance.
Summaries that can be produced by at least one dataset satisfying all the stated restrictions.
Records that may be any real numbers, including negative values and non-integers.
The non-negative total \(D=\sum(x-\mu)^2=Q-\frac{T^2}{n}\).
The boundary case where the centred sum of squares is zero, forcing every record to equal the mean.
One algebraic value for the number of records, which must be checked as a positive integer and against the original summaries.
One possible sign of the mean after recovering its square; each sign has its own total and any related coding origin.
The unknown value \(c\) used to code each observation as \(x-c\).
A condition every allowed dataset must satisfy. Passing it alone may not prove that the dataset exists.
A condition that guarantees existence under the assumptions stated with it.

examples.title: Test a proposed sum of squares
examples.question: Three unrestricted real observations have total \(T=6\). Determine whether each proposed sum of squares \(Q=10,12,14\) is possible. Give a possible dataset when it exists, and find the variance when \(Q=14\).
solution:
\[\mu=\frac{6}{3}=2,\qquad D=Q-\frac{6^2}{3}=Q-12.\]

A centred sum of squares cannot be negative.
For \(Q=10\), \(D=-2\), so no real dataset exists. For \(Q=12\), \(D=0\), so all observations must equal \(2\): the list is \(2,2,2\).
For \(Q=14\), one possible list is \(1,2,3\). It has total \(6\) and sum of squares \(1+4+9=14\).

\[V=\frac{14}{3}-2^2=\frac{2}{3}.\]

A possible list proves existence; the moment totals do not generally recover a unique original dataset.

examples.title: Keep both feasible counts
examples.question: Unrestricted real observations have total \(T=12\), sum of squares \(Q=60\) and descriptive variance \(6\). Find every possible positive integer count. Then select the count if the mean is known to exceed \(\frac{5}{2}\).
solution: Both are feasible positive integer counts. For example, \(1,1,3,7\) works for four records, and \(0,0,1,1,3,7\) works for six. Both lists have total \(12\) and sum of squares \(60\).
Without the additional condition, retain both counts. Requiring \(\mu>\frac{5}{2}\) selects \(n=4\), whose mean is \(3\).

examples.title: Recover a mean from its square
examples.question: Four unrestricted real observations have sum of squares \(148\) and descriptive variance \(12\). Find every possible mean and corresponding total. Explain which branch could remain if all observations must be non-negative.
solution:
\[T=4\mu=20\text{ or }-20.\]

Keep each total with its corresponding mean.

Both real branches are feasible. One positive-mean example is

\[5-2\sqrt{6},\quad5,\quad5,\quad5+2\sqrt{6}.\]

Its total is \(20\), centred sum of squares is \(48\), and original sum of squares is \(148\). Negating all four records gives the negative branch.
Non-negative observations cannot have mean \(-5\). The positive example is itself non-negative because \(5>2\sqrt{6}\), so mean \(5\) remains feasible under that extra condition.

examples.title: Recover both an unknown mean and a hidden origin
examples.question:
Five numerical observations have original sum of squares \(Q=65\). Relative to an unknown origin \(c\),

\[D_c=10,\qquad E_c=40.\]

Find all pairs \((c,\mu)\), and check each against both moments. Then select the pair if \(c>0\).
solution:
The original sum of squares must satisfy \(Q=E_c+2cD_c+nc^2\). For the two origins,

\[c=1:\quad40+2(1)(10)+5(1^2)=65,\]\[c=-5:\quad40+2(-5)(10)+5(-5)^2=65.\]
Both first moments also satisfy \(D_c=5(\mu-c)=10\). Example lists are \(0,2,3,4,6\) for \(c=1\), and \(-6,-4,-3,-2,0\) for \(c=-5\). The extra condition \(c>0\) selects \((c,\mu)=(1,3)\).

examples.title: Apply restrictions to the actual records
examples.question: Consider two separate proposals. A has \(n=3,T=4,Q=18\). B has \(n=2,T=5,Q=14\). For A, decide whether real records and non-negative records are possible. For B, compare non-negative real records with non-negative integer counts.
solution: A has a real witness \(-1,1,4\), with total \(4\) and sum of squares \(18\). However, non-negative records would require \(Q\le T^2=16\), so A cannot satisfy that restriction.

For B, let the observations be \(a,b\). Then

\[a+b=5,\qquad a^2+b^2=14,\qquad ab=\frac{25-14}{2}=\frac{11}{2}.\]

\[z^2-5z+\frac{11}{2}=0\Longrightarrow z=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{3}}{2}.\]

Both values are positive, so non-negative real records exist.
The non-negative integer pairs with total \(5\), up to order, are \((0,5),(1,4),(2,3)\). Their sums of squares are \(25,17,13\). None gives \(14\), so integer counts are impossible.

related.title: Coded totals, origins and scale changes

extraPractice.title: Two counts can describe the same totals
extraPractice.prompt: A nonempty list of real observations has total \(T=24\), sum of squares \(Q=144\) and descriptive variance \(V=8\). Find every possible number of observations. Then find the count and mean if additional information says that the mean exceeds \(3\).

fields.label: Count when the mean exceeds three

extraPractice.hint: The count occurs in both denominators of \(V=\frac{Q}{n}-\left(\frac{T}{n}\right)^2\). Clear both denominators and retain all feasible positive integer roots before using the extra condition.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[8n^2-144n+24^2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad8(n-6)(n-12)=0.\]

  2. Both \(n=6\) and \(n=12\) are positive integers greater than one. They give non-negative centred sums of squares and the stated variance.

  3. For \(n=6\), a confirming list is \(0,2,2,6,6,8\). For \(n=12\), eight zeros and four sixes have the same total and sum of squares. Thus both counts really can occur.

  4. \[\bar{x}=\frac{24}{6}=4\quad\text{or}\quad\bar{x}=\frac{24}{12}=2.\]

  5. The condition \(\bar{x}>3\) selects \(n=6\) and mean \(4\).

extraPractice.title: Keep both signs until the condition selects one
extraPractice.prompt: Five real observations have sum of squares \(85\) and descriptive variance \(8\). Find every possible mean. If their total is negative, find the mean and total.

fields.label: Mean when the total is negative

extraPractice.hint: First calculate the square of the mean. A sum of squares does not by itself determine the sign of the mean.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}^{\,2}=\frac{85}{5}-8=9\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bar{x}=-3\text{ or }3.\]

  2. The list \(-1,1,3,5,7\) confirms the positive mean: its total is \(15\), sum of squares is \(85\), and variance is \(8\). Negating every record gives the negative-mean case without changing the sum of squares or variance.

  3. A negative total and positive count require a negative mean. Therefore

    \[\bar{x}=-3,\qquad T=5(-3)=-15.\]

extraPractice.title: A real-data bound need not be attainable by integers
extraPractice.prompt: A report claims that four real observations have \(T=10\) and \(Q=24\). Calculate the implied variance and explain whether the report is possible. Find the smallest possible \(Q\) for four real observations with total \(10\). Can this minimum be attained if all four observations must be integers?

options.no: No: the implied variance is negative.
options.yes: Yes: a negative mean can cause negative variance.

fields.label: Minimum sum of squares for real observations
Can integer observations attain this minimum?

options.no: No: equality requires every record to equal \(\frac{5}{2}\).
options.yes: Yes: integer totals guarantee integer observations.

extraPractice.hint: Use \(Q\ge\frac{T^2}{n}\). At equality, every observation must equal the mean.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[V=\frac{24}{4}-\left(\frac{10}{4}\right)^2=6-\frac{25}{4}=-\frac{1}{4}.\]

  2. The report is impossible because a sum of squared deviations cannot be negative.

  3. \[Q\ge\frac{10^2}{4}=25.\]

  4. The real-data minimum is attained by four copies of \(\frac{5}{2}\). Equality forces this constant list, so no integer list can attain \(Q=25\). For comparison, \(2,2,3,3\) is an integer list with the required total and \(Q=26\).

extraPractice.title: An origin must satisfy both coded totals
extraPractice.prompt: Seven real observations have mean \(10\), \(\sum(x-c)=-21\) and \(\sum(x-c)^2=91\). Find the unknown origin \(c\), original descriptive variance and SD, original total and original sum of squares. Explain why \(c=7\) cannot replace your answer even though it gives the same squared total for this dataset.
extraPractice.hint: The first coded total fixes which side of the mean the origin lies on. Then use the coded variance, which is unchanged by translation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[-21=7(10-c)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=13.\]
  2. \[V=\frac{91}{7}-\left(\frac{-21}{7}\right)^2=13-9=4,\qquad \sigma=2.\]
  3. \[T=7(10)=70,\qquad Q=7(4+10^2)=728.\]

  4. The coded totals check directly from the reconstructed moments:

    \[T-7c=70-91=-21,\]\[Q-2cT+7c^2=728-2(13)(70)+7(13^2)=91.\]

  5. Using \(c=7\) would give first coded total \(70-49=21\), which contradicts the stated negative total. The squared total alone cannot select between references equally far from the mean.

extraPractice.title: Handle a single observation and zero variance separately
extraPractice.prompt:
Each case below describes a separate nonempty list of real observations. Decide the possible number of records in each case.

A: \(T=0,\ Q=4,\ V=4\).
B: \(T=6,\ Q=36,\ V=0\).
C: \(T=0,\ Q=0,\ V=0\).
extraPractice.hint: The count equation is a necessary algebraic condition. A single record has zero variance. When all three summaries are zero, do not divide by a zero coefficient.
extraPractice.solution:
1. For A,

    \[4n^2-4n=4n(n-1)=0.\]

    The candidate \(n=0\) is not a nonempty list. For \(n=1\), total zero forces the only record to be zero, so its sum of squares and variance would both be zero. Thus \(n=1\) also fails, and A has no feasible count.

  2. For B, the count equation becomes

    \[-36n+36=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=1.\]

    The single observation \(6\) has exactly the stated moments and zero variance.

  3. For C, the equation is \(0=0\). Any positive number of zero observations has total zero, sum of squares zero and variance zero. Hence every positive integer count is feasible.

starters.title: Reject a fractional count before coding the records
starters.question: A nonempty list of real observations has \(T=9\), \(Q=45\) and descriptive variance \(6\). Find both algebraic candidates for its count, then identify every feasible count. Find the mean and exact SD. The observations are coded by \(u=\frac{x-5}{2}\); find \(\sum u\) and \(\sum u^2\).
starters.hint: Clear denominators in the variance equation. Keep both algebraic candidates long enough to explain which fails the count condition. Expand the coding square before summing.
starters.solution:
1. \[6n^2-45n+81=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3(n-3)(2n-9)=0.\]

  2. The algebraic candidates are \(3\) and \(\frac{9}{2}\). Only \(n=3\) is an integer count. It is feasible: the list \(0,3,6\) has \(T=9\), \(Q=45\) and variance \(6\).

  3. \[\bar{x}=\frac{9}{3}=3,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{6}.\]
  4. \[\sum u=\frac{T-5n}{2}=\frac{9-15}{2}=-3.\]
  5. \[\sum u^2=\frac{Q-10T+25n}{4}=\frac{45-90+75}{4}=\frac{15}{2}.\]

  6. A final scale check gives

    \[V_u=\frac{\frac{15}{2}}{3}-\left(\frac{-3}{3}\right)^2=\frac{3}{2},\qquad V_x=2^2\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)=6.\]
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the count equation from both moment terms.
  • 1 mark: solve for both algebraic candidates.
  • 1 mark: reject the fractional count and verify the integer count is feasible.
  • 1 mark: obtain the original mean and exact SD.
  • 1 mark: calculate the coded first total.
  • 1 mark: expand the coded square and calculate its total.
  • 1 mark: verify the original variance through the coding scale.

starters.title: Match each mean sign to its own origin
starters.question: Four real observations have \(Q=116\), descriptive variance \(4\) and \(D_c=\sum(x-c)=-12\), where the origin \(c\) is unknown. Find every ordered pair \((\bar{x},c)\), then select the pair if \(c>0\). Calculate the required squared coded total \(E_c=\sum(x-c)^2\). Could a separate report with the same \(n,Q,V,D_c\) but \(E_c=48\) be correct?
starters.hint: Recover both signs of the mean from \(Q\) and the variance. Then use \(D_c=n(\bar{x}-c)\) for each branch. Translation must leave the variance unchanged.
starters.solution:
1. \[\bar{x}^{\,2}=\frac{116}{4}-4=25\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bar{x}=\pm5.\]
  2. \[-12=4(\bar{x}-c)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=\bar{x}+3.\]

    The pairs are \((-5,-2)\) and \((5,8)\). The lists \(-7,-7,-3,-3\) and \(3,3,7,7\) confirm that both branches can occur.

  3. The condition \(c>0\) selects \((\bar{x},c)=(5,8)\).

  4. \[E_c=nV+\frac{D_c^2}{n}=4(4)+\frac{(-12)^2}{4}=52.\]

  5. This value is the same on both branches because each origin lies three above its own mean. For example, the positive-mean branch gives

    \[E_8=116-2(8)(20)+4(8^2)=52.\]

  6. The separate report would imply

    \[V=\frac{48}{4}-\left(\frac{-12}{4}\right)^2=12-9=3.\]

    That contradicts the stated variance \(4\), so no choice of origin can repair it while keeping the other summaries unchanged.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: recover both possible signs of the mean.
  • 1 mark: derive the matching origin for each sign.
  • 1 mark: verify both branches and apply the positive-origin condition.
  • 1 mark: recover the required squared coded total.
  • 1 mark: check that coded total against the original moments.
  • 1 mark: identify the variance contradiction in the separate report.

revision.body:
Recover every algebraic candidate, then check whether the original records can exist.

Can these moments describe real observations?

Let \(n\) be a positive integer, \(T=\sum x\), and \(Q=\sum x^2\).

\[\bar{x}=\frac{T}{n},\qquad V=\frac{Q}{n}-\left(\frac{T}{n}\right)^2,\qquad Q\ge\frac{T^2}{n}.\]

For \(n\ge2\), this bound is sufficient for unrestricted real records. Equality forces every record to equal \(\bar{x}\). For \(n=1\), require \(Q=T^2\) and \(V=0\); the inequality alone is insufficient.

How many observations are possible?

\[Vn^2-Qn+T^2=0.\]

Keep every positive integer root, then check the original moments and all stated conditions. A positive fractional root is not a count. A single record cannot have positive variance.

If \(V=0\) and \(Q>0\), use \(n=\frac{T^2}{Q}\) and check the count. If \(T=Q=V=0\), every positive integer count works: all records are zero. Other incompatible zero-moment claims must be rejected.

Which mean and origin branches survive?

\[\bar{x}^{\,2}=\frac{Q}{n}-V,\qquad D_c=n(\bar{x}-c),\qquad E_c=nV+\frac{D_c^2}{n}.\]

A positive mean-square gives two signs; zero gives one mean; a negative result is impossible. Pair each mean with \(c=\bar{x}-\frac{D_c}{n}\). Check both coded totals, then apply any condition on the mean or origin.

Do the records satisfy the context?

Counts are positive integers even when measurements may be real. If observations must be non-negative, then \(T\ge0\) and \(Q\le T^2\) are additional necessary checks. Integer records need further checks: a real witness may not be an integer witness.

Keep exact values until the final answer. Give every valid branch, or explain the specific contradiction if none survives.
revision.checks:
• All roots and signs retained before applying the stated conditions?
  • Single-record and zero-variance cases checked separately?
  • Original moments, record restrictions and units all satisfied?
