orig_9709_s1_var_changes_combining.description: Track the count, total and sum of squares when records change or groups are joined. Explain where pooled spread comes from, recover a missing group, and solve conditions that preserve or limit the standard deviation.

sections.title: What changes when a record is corrected, added or removed?
sections.label: Update the records
sections.intro:
Track three quantities: the positive integer count \(n\), total \(T=\sum x\), and sum of squares \(Q=\sum x^2\). The descriptive summaries are

\[\mu=\frac{T}{n},\qquad V=\frac{Q}{n}-\mu^2,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{V}.\]

Variance uses squared data units; SD uses the original units. A supplied SD must be squared before using \(Q=n(V+\mu^2)\).

ChangeNew countNew totalNew sum of squares
Replace one \(r\) by \(t\)\(n\)\(T-r+t\)\(Q-r^2+t^2\)
Add one \(z\)\(n+1\)\(T+z\)\(Q+z^2\)
Remove one existing \(r\)\(n-1\)\(T-r\)\(Q-r^2\)

Recalculate from the new totals and count. Mean and variance require a nonempty remaining list. If an entry is an accidental duplicate, remove one extra copy only.

blocks.html: The change in the sum of squares is \(t^2-r^2\), not \((t-r)^2\). A replacement keeps the number of records fixed; an addition or removal does not.

blocks.title: Update the corrected list before removing a record
blocks.prompt: The records are \(2,3,7,8\). First correct \(8\) to \(10\). Find the corrected count, mean and descriptive variance. Then remove the record \(3\) from that corrected list and find the remaining variance.
blocks.hint: The replacement keeps the count fixed. The later removal starts from the corrected totals and reduces the count by one.
blocks.solution:
1. \[n=4,\qquad T=20,\qquad Q=126.\]
  2. \[T_{\mathrm{new}}=20-8+10=22,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{new}}=126-8^2+10^2=162.\]
  3. \[\mu_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{22}{4}=\frac{11}{2},\qquad V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{162}{4}-\left(\frac{11}{2}\right)^2=\frac{41}{4}.\]

  4. After removing the record \(3\), the list is \(2,7,10\), with

    \[n=3,\quad T=19,\quad Q=153,\quad V=\frac{153}{3}-\left(\frac{19}{3}\right)^2=\frac{98}{9}.\]

sections.title: How do I pool two groups on the same original scale?
sections.label: Pool the moments
sections.intro:
Pooling joins two disjoint lists: each observation appears once, although different records may have equal values. For each group, reconstruct

\[T_i=n_i\mu_i,\qquad Q_i=n_i(V_i+\mu_i^2).\]

Then add counts and moment totals:

\[N=n_A+n_B,\quad T=T_A+T_B,\quad Q=Q_A+Q_B,\]\[\mu=\frac{T}{N},\qquad V=\frac{Q}{N}-\mu^2,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{V}.\]

The mean is weighted by group size. An unweighted average of two means works when their counts are equal or their means are equal. An average of SDs is not a pooling rule.

blocks.html:
Restore each code and unit first. If \(u=\frac{x-a}{b}\), where \(b\ne0\), write \(x=a+bu\). Then

\[T_x=na+b\sum u,\]\[Q_x=na^2+2ab\sum u+b^2\sum u^2.\]

For a unit conversion \(y=cx\), multiply the total by \(c\) and the sum of squares and variance by \(c^2\). Use a single common original scale before pooling.

blocks.title: Decode one group before pooling
blocks.prompt: Group A contains three observations coded by \(u=\frac{x-2}{2}\), with \(\sum u=3\) and \(\sum u^2=5\). Disjoint group B contains two observations on the original scale, with mean \(7\) and descriptive variance \(1\). Find the combined mean and variance.
blocks.hint: Write \(x=2+2u\). Recover A’s original total and sum of squares, reconstruct B’s moments, then pool the two lists.

blocks.html: This joins observed records. It does not form pairwise sums of observations or use a rule for adding random variables. Disjoint groups may still contain repeated values.

sections.title: Why can combined spread exceed both group spreads?
sections.label: Within and between
sections.intro:
Each record differs from the pooled mean because of its position inside its group and the position of that group’s mean. For two groups,

\[V=\underbrace{\frac{n_AV_A+n_BV_B}{N}}_{\text{within groups}}+\underbrace{\frac{n_A(\mu_A-\mu)^2+n_B(\mu_B-\mu)^2}{N}}_{\text{between groups}}.\]

The between-group term also equals

\[\frac{n_An_B}{N^2}(\mu_A-\mu_B)^2.\]

It is non-negative and becomes zero when the group means agree. Then the combined variance is a weighted average of the variances; the combined SD is its square root.

blocks.html:
\[\bar x=\frac{4(5)+6(10)}{10}=8,\qquad W=\frac4{10}(4)+\frac6{10}(4)=4.\]\[B=\frac4{10}(5-8)^2+\frac6{10}(10-8)^2=6.\]\[V_{\mathrm{pooled}}=W+B=10,\qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{pooled}}=\sqrt{10}.\]

The two within-group variances are equal. The separated group means add a further contribution.

The original groups \(3,3,7,7\) and \(8,8,8,12,12,12\) each have variance \(4\). Their pooled mean is \(8\), and pooled variance is \(4+6=10\).

blocks.title: Separate internal spread from separated centres
blocks.prompt: Group A has two observations with mean \(3\) and variance \(4\). Disjoint group B has six observations with mean \(7\) and variance \(4\). Find the within-group contribution, between-group contribution and combined variance.
blocks.hint: Weight the two variances by their counts. Add the contribution from the difference between the group means.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=8,\qquad \mu=\frac{2(3)+6(7)}{8}=6.\]
  2. \[W=\frac{2(4)+6(4)}{8}=4.\]
  3. \[B=\frac{2\cdot6}{8^2}(3-7)^2=3.\]
  4. \[V=W+B=7.\]

    Both groups have SD \(2\), but their combined SD is \(\sqrt{7}\) because their means differ.

sections.title: Can I recover a hidden group by subtraction?
sections.label: Recover a group
sections.intro:
If the complete dataset is exactly A together with B, subtract A’s count, total and sum of squares:

\[n_B=N-n_A,\quad T_B=T-T_A,\quad Q_B=Q-Q_A.\]

For a positive remaining count, calculate \(\mu_B=\frac{T_B}{n_B}\) and \(V_B=\frac{Q_B}{n_B}-\mu_B^2\). Check whether the records can exist:

  • For \(n_B\ge2\), unrestricted real records require \(Q_B\ge\frac{T_B^2}{n_B}\); this condition is also sufficient.
  • For \(n_B=1\), require \(Q_B=T_B^2\) and zero variance.
  • For \(n_B=0\), both remaining totals must be zero. The remainder is empty, so its mean, variance and SD are undefined.

A negative or non-integer remaining count is invalid. Apply any extra integer or non-negative record restrictions as well.

blocks.title: Check the last remaining observation
blocks.prompt: A proposed complete dataset has \(N=5,T=21,Q=99\). A known subgroup has \(n_A=4,T_A=16,Q_A=76\). Find the remaining count, total and sum of squares, then decide whether the claim that A is a subgroup is possible. Separately, if subtraction leaves no records and both remaining totals are zero, what can be said about the remaining mean and SD?

fields.label: Can these summaries describe the claimed subgroup relation?

options.no: No: the single remaining value cannot have the proposed sum of squares.
options.yes: Yes: the calculated variance is non-negative.
options.zero: Yes: assign the remaining value zero.

fields.label: Mean and SD of an empty remainder

options.undefined: Neither is defined for the empty list.
options.same: They equal the original mean and SD.

blocks.hint: Subtract all three summaries. A single value with total \(t\) must have sum of squares \(t^2\). An empty remainder has count zero, so its mean and SD are undefined.
blocks.solution:
1. \[n_B=5-4=1,\qquad T_B=21-16=5,\qquad Q_B=99-76=23.\]

  2. The single remaining observation would be \(5\), so its square would be \(25\), not \(23\). The subgroup claim is impossible.

  3. An empty remainder is consistent only if both remaining totals are zero. Its mean, variance and SD are undefined because there are no observations.

blocks.html: Show the recovered count, total and sum of squares before calculating the hidden SD. A negative implied variance signals incompatible summaries; taking an absolute value would not repair the data.

sections.title: Which new values preserve or change the SD?
sections.label: Add one record
sections.intro:
Suppose the original list has \(n\ge1\), mean \(\mu\) and descriptive variance \(V\). After adding one real value \(z\),

\[\mu_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{n\mu+z}{n+1},\]\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{n}{n+1}V+\frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(z-\mu)^2.\]

This follows by substituting \(T=n\mu\) and \(Q=n(V+\mu^2)\) into the new moment formula. At \(z=\mu\), the mean stays fixed and positive variance decreases by the factor \(\frac{n}{n+1}\); zero variance stays zero.

To preserve SD, set \(V_{\mathrm{new}}=V\). Rearranging gives

\[(z-\mu)^2=\frac{n+1}{n}V.\]

There are two real additions when \(V>0\), and the single addition \(z=\mu\) when \(V=0\). Check both branches against the question’s record restrictions.

blocks.html:
After adding \(z\), the count is \(5\), the total \(20+z\) and the sum of squares \(120+z^2\).

\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{120+z^2}{5}-\left(\frac{20+z}{5}\right)^2=4+\frac4{25}(z-5)^2.\]\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=5\Longrightarrow(z-5)^2=\frac{25}{4}\Longrightarrow z=5\pm\frac52.\]
Added valueNew meanNew SD
\(\frac52\)\(\frac92\)\(\sqrt5\)
\(\frac{15}2\)\(\frac{11}2\)\(\sqrt5\)

Adding \(\frac{5}{2}\) or \(\frac{15}{2}\) to \(2,4,6,8\) preserves variance \(5\), while changing the mean to \(\frac{9}{2}\) or \(\frac{11}{2}\).

blocks.title: Find both additions that preserve SD
blocks.prompt: The original records are \(0,0,3\). Add one real observation \(z\) so that the descriptive SD remains unchanged. Find every possible \(z\), then select the value if all records must be non-negative.
blocks.hint: First find the original mean and variance. Equal non-negative SDs have equal variances, so use the addition identity and retain both square-root signs.
blocks.solution:
1. \[n=3,\qquad\mu=1,\qquad V=\frac{9}{3}-1^2=2.\]
  2. \[V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{3}{4}(2)+\frac{3}{16}(z-1)^2.\]
  3. \[V_{\mathrm{new}}=2\Longrightarrow(z-1)^2=\frac{8}{3}\Longrightarrow z=1\pm\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}.\]

  4. Both real values preserve the variance and hence the SD. Since \(\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}>1\), the minus branch is negative. Non-negative records therefore require \(z=1+\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}\).

sections.title: How do I control spread when a symmetric pair moves?
sections.label: Symmetric changes
sections.intro:
Suppose two existing records are \(\mu-d\) and \(\mu+d\), where \(d\ge0\) and \(\mu\) is the whole list’s mean. Replace them by \(\mu-(d+t)\) and \(\mu+(d+t)\), with \(t\ge0\). Their sum is unchanged, so the count and mean stay fixed. The increase in centred sum of squares is

\[2(d+t)^2-2d^2=4dt+2t^2.\]

Therefore, for the original count \(n\ge2\),

\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=V+\frac{4dt+2t^2}{n}.\]

For an SD bound \(\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}\le s\), first check \(s\ge0\), then solve \(V_{\mathrm{new}}\le s^2\). A negative bound is impossible. Intersect the algebraic answer with \(t\ge0\) and any restrictions on the changed records. Keep or exclude endpoints according to the stated inequality.

blocks.title: Apply the SD bound and then the record constraint
blocks.prompt: The records \(1,4,4,7\) have their outer pair replaced by \(1-t,7+t\), where \(t\ge0\). Find the greatest allowed \(t\) if the new SD must not exceed \(3\). Then impose the additional condition that every record is non-negative and give the new greatest allowed \(t\).
blocks.hint: The mean stays at \(4\). The changed pair has deviations \(\pm(3+t)\), while the other two deviations are zero.
blocks.solution:
1. \[V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{2(3+t)^2}{4}=\frac{(3+t)^2}{2}.\]

  2. Both the SD and its bound are non-negative, so

    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}\le3\Longleftrightarrow\frac{(3+t)^2}{2}\le9.\]

  3. Since \(t\ge0\), \(3+t>0\). Thus

    \[0\le t\le3\sqrt{2}-3.\]

  4. The additional record constraint requires \(1-t\ge0\), hence \(t\le1\). Since \(3\sqrt{2}-3>1\), the final allowed interval is \(0\le t\le1\).

glossary.definition: Correcting one recorded value while retaining the same number of observations.
The total \(Q=\sum x^2\), obtained by squaring each observation before adding.
Two groups with no shared observation records. Different records are still allowed to have equal numerical values.
The single list formed by joining the records from the two groups.
The same measurement units and original variable after each group’s code has been reversed.
The count-weighted contribution from variation around each group’s own mean.
The additional variance caused by differences between the group means.
The remaining records after a known subgroup has been removed from the complete dataset.
A list containing exactly one observation, which necessarily has zero descriptive variance.
Two records \(\mu-d\) and \(\mu+d\), equally far from the whole dataset’s mean.

examples.title: A correction, an addition and a removal are different operations
examples.question: Start with \(2,6,6,10\). Find the new mean and variance for each separate change: replace \(10\) by \(14\); add one new record \(6\); remove one of the two records \(6\). Each change starts from the original list.
solution: The addition and removal preserve the mean but change the variance. One repeated value is one record; removing one copy does not remove every occurrence.

examples.title: Restore the original scale, then pool the moments
examples.question: Group A consists of four coded values \(1,1,3,3\), where \(u=\frac{x-1}{2}\). Disjoint group B consists of the six original values \(8,8,8,12,12,12\). Find the combined mean and descriptive SD on the original scale.
solution: The two original SDs are both \(2\), but their pooled SD is \(\sqrt{10}\). The distinct group means contribute additional spread.

examples.title: Zero spread inside each group can still give pooled variation
examples.question: Group A contains three copies of \(2\). Group B contains two copies of \(7\). Calculate their within-group and between-group contributions to the combined variance.
solution:
Each group is constant, so \(V_A=V_B=0\). The combined mean is

\[\mu=\frac{3(2)+2(7)}{5}=4.\]

\[V=W+B=6,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{6}.\]

All the pooled variation comes from the separation between the group means. Averaging the two zero SDs would miss it completely.

examples.title: Subtract a known group from the whole dataset
examples.question: A complete dataset has \(N=7,T=40,Q=260\). A known subgroup A has three observations, mean \(4\) and descriptive variance \(\frac{8}{3}\). Find the count, mean and variance of the remaining group B, and check its moment feasibility.
solution:
\[Q_B-\frac{T_B^2}{n_B}=204-196=8\ge0.\]

Four unrestricted real observations can have these moments. For example, \(5,7,7,9\) has total \(28\) and sum of squares \(204\).
Combining this example with A’s possible list \(2,4,6\) restores the complete count and both original totals.

examples.title: Add a value while keeping the same SD
examples.question: The records are \(2,4,6,8\). Find every real value \(z\) that can be added without changing the descriptive SD. Give the corresponding new means.
solution:
Equal SDs give equal variances. The addition identity gives

\[5=\frac{4}{5}(5)+\frac{4}{25}(z-5)^2.\]
Substitution in the addition identity gives variance \(5\) for both branches. Inserting the old mean \(5\) instead would give variance \(4\), so it would not preserve the original SD.

examples.title: Move a symmetric pair and enforce a spread limit
examples.question: The records are \(1,3,7,9\). Replace the pair \(1,9\) by \(1-t,9+t\), with \(t\ge0\), keeping the other records fixed. Find all \(t\) for which the new SD does not exceed \(4\). Then require every record to be non-negative.
solution:
The original mean is \(5\), and the pair has deviations \(\pm4\). Its sum remains \(10\), so the mean stays fixed. Initially,

\[V=\frac{16+4+4+16}{4}=10.\]

The SD bound is non-negative, so squaring is valid:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}\le4\Longleftrightarrow10+4t+\frac{t^2}{2}\le16.\]

Non-negative records also require \(1-t\ge0\). Since \(2\sqrt{7}-4>1\), the final interval is

\[0\le t\le1.\]
At \(t=1\), the records are \(0,3,7,10\), with variance \(\frac{29}{2}<16\), confirming that the included endpoint meets the SD condition.

extraPractice.title: Replace the erroneous square as well as the record
extraPractice.prompt: Five numerical readings have total \(30\) and sum of squares \(254\). One recorded reading of \(12\) should have been \(7\). Find the corrected mean, descriptive variance and exact SD.
extraPractice.hint: The number of records stays the same. Remove \(12\) from the total and \(12^2\) from the sum of squares, then insert \(7\) and \(7^2\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[n=5,\qquad T_{\mathrm{new}}=30-12+7=25.\]
  2. \[Q_{\mathrm{new}}=254-12^2+7^2=254-144+49=159.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{25}{5}=5,\qquad V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{159}{5}-5^2=\frac{34}{5}.\]
  4. \[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}=\sqrt{\frac{34}{5}}=\frac{\sqrt{170}}{5}.\]

  5. The change in the sum of squares is \(7^2-12^2=-95\). It is not the square of the correction, \((7-12)^2=25\).

extraPractice.title: Distinguish removing a record from adding the old mean
extraPractice.prompt: The original numerical list is \(4,4,7,9\). First remove just one record equal to \(4\): find the remaining count, mean and descriptive variance. In a separate experiment, start again from the original four records and add their original mean as one new record. Find this second list’s mean and variance.
extraPractice.hint: Keep a separate ledger for each experiment. Removing one repeated record does not remove every record with that value. Adding a record at the old mean changes the count but not the mean.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The original moments are

    \[n=4,\quad T=24,\quad Q=162,\quad\bar{x}=6,\quad V=\frac{162}{4}-6^2=\frac{9}{2}.\]

  2. After removing one \(4\),

    \[n_{\mathrm{r}}=3,\quad T_{\mathrm{r}}=20,\quad Q_{\mathrm{r}}=146.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{20}{3},\qquad V_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{146}{3}-\left(\frac{20}{3}\right)^2=\frac{38}{9}.\]

  4. For the separate addition, the new record is the original mean \(6\), so

    \[n_{\mathrm{a}}=5,\quad T_{\mathrm{a}}=30,\quad Q_{\mathrm{a}}=198.\]
  5. \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{a}}=6,\qquad V_{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{198}{5}-6^2=\frac{18}{5}=\frac{4}{5}\left(\frac{9}{2}\right).\]

  6. The added record contributes zero deviation from the unchanged mean. The same total squared deviation is now divided among five records, so this positive variance decreases.

extraPractice.title: Separate variation within and between two groups
extraPractice.prompt: Two disjoint groups of numerical observations use the same scale. A has count \(4\), mean \(10\) and descriptive variance \(4\). B has count \(6\), mean \(15\) and descriptive variance \(9\). Find the pooled mean, the within-group and between-group contributions to pooled variance, the pooled variance and the exact pooled SD.
extraPractice.hint: Weight each group by its number of records. The differences between the group means and the pooled mean supply an additional non-negative contribution.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N=10,\qquad\bar{x}=\frac{4(10)+6(15)}{10}=13.\]
  2. \[V_{\mathrm{within}}=\frac{4(4)+6(9)}{10}=7.\]
  3. \[V_{\mathrm{between}}=\frac{4(10-13)^2+6(15-13)^2}{10}=6.\]
  4. \[V=7+6=13,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{13}.\]

  5. The original moments verify this independently:

    \[T=130,\quad Q=4(4+10^2)+6(9+15^2)=1820,\]\[V=\frac{1820}{10}-13^2=13.\]

  6. The two group SDs are \(2\) and \(3\), while \(\sqrt{13}>3\). Pooling can give greater spread than either group because their centres differ.

extraPractice.title: Recover a missing group by subtraction of moments
extraPractice.prompt: Eight numerical observations have mean \(9\) and descriptive variance \(\frac{39}{4}\). Three of them form group A, with mean \(6\) and descriptive variance \(\frac{8}{3}\). Find the count, mean and variance of the remaining group B. The two groups are disjoint and together contain all eight records.
extraPractice.hint: Recover counts, totals and sums of squares for the whole set and A, then subtract. Variances themselves are not additive.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T=8(9)=72,\qquad Q=8\left(\frac{39}{4}+9^2\right)=726.\]
  2. \[T_A=3(6)=18,\qquad Q_A=3\left(\frac{8}{3}+6^2\right)=116.\]
  3. \[n_B=8-3=5,\qquad T_B=72-18=54,\qquad Q_B=726-116=610.\]
  4. \[\bar{x}_B=\frac{54}{5},\qquad V_B=\frac{610}{5}-\left(\frac{54}{5}\right)^2=\frac{134}{25}.\]

  5. A confirming example is A: \(4,6,8\), and B: \(8,9,10,13,14\). The groups are feasible and reproduce the combined moments. Simply subtracting the two supplied variances would not recover \(V_B\).

extraPractice.title: Retain both additions that preserve the SD
extraPractice.prompt: Four numerical observations have mean \(10\) and descriptive variance \(16\). Find every real value \(z\) that can be added as one new observation without changing the SD. If \(z>10\), select the new observation and find the new mean. Separately, if the original four records all equal \(10\), which added value preserves their zero SD?

fields.label: All added values for the positive-variance case
Added value exceeding the old mean
New mean for that selected value
Added value for the separate zero-SD case

extraPractice.hint: Equal non-negative SDs are equivalent to equal variances. Solve the squared distance from the old mean and keep both signs before applying \(z>10\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[16=\frac{4}{5}(16)+\frac{4}{25}(z-10)^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(z-10)^2=20.\]
  2. \[z=10\pm2\sqrt{5}.\]

    Both values give the required variance and SD.

  3. The condition \(z>10\) selects \(10+2\sqrt{5}\). Its new mean is

    \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{40+10+2\sqrt{5}}{5}=10+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}.\]

  4. For the separate constant original list, zero SD after addition requires all five values to agree. Hence only \(z=10\) works; there are not two distinct branches.

starters.title: Decode two groups, then correct one original reading
starters.question: Two disjoint groups contain masses \(x\), in grams. A uses \(u=\frac{x-20}{2}\) and has \(n_A=4\), \(\sum u=4\), \(\sum u^2=12\). B uses \(v=\frac{x-30}{-2}\) and has \(n_B=6\), \(\sum v=6\), \(\sum v^2=10\). Find the pooled original mean and descriptive variance. One original mass of \(26\,\mathrm{g}\) in B was then found to be a transcription error for \(22\,\mathrm{g}\). Find the corrected pooled mean, variance and exact SD.
starters.hint: The two coded lists use different origins and opposite scales, so first recover both groups on the original gram scale. Replace the erroneous original mass and its square only after the scales agree.
starters.solution:
1. For A, \(x=20+2u\), giving

    \[T_A=4(20)+2(4)=88,\]\[Q_A=4(20^2)+2(20)(2)(4)+2^2(12)=1968.\]

  2. For B, \(x=30-2v\), giving

    \[T_B=6(30)-2(6)=168,\]\[Q_B=6(30^2)+2(30)(-2)(6)+(-2)^2(10)=4720.\]
  3. \[N=10,\quad T=256,\quad Q=6688,\quad\bar{x}=\frac{128}{5}\,\mathrm{g}.\]
  4. \[V=\frac{6688}{10}-\left(\frac{128}{5}\right)^2=\frac{336}{25}\,\mathrm{g}^2.\]

  5. The correction keeps the total count at ten:

    \[T_{\mathrm{new}}=256-26+22=252,\]\[Q_{\mathrm{new}}=6688-26^2+22^2=6496.\]
  6. \[\bar{x}_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{126}{5}\,\mathrm{g},\qquad V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{6496}{10}-\left(\frac{126}{5}\right)^2=\frac{364}{25}\,\mathrm{g}^2.\]
  7. \[\sigma_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{2\sqrt{91}}{5}\,\mathrm{g}.\]

    The corrected mean decreases, but the variance increases. A change in the total alone does not determine what happens to spread.

starters.title: Use an SD bound on symmetric outward changes
starters.question: The original numerical observations are \(2,5,5,8\). Replace the first and last records by \(2-t\) and \(8+t\), where \(t\ge0\). Observations are allowed to be any real numbers. Find the new mean and the formula for descriptive variance \(V(t)\). The new SD must be at most \(4\). Find the two real roots of the boundary equation before applying the domain, then give the complete allowed interval for \(t\). Finally, list all allowed values if the adjustment \(t\) is also required to be an integer.
starters.hint: The pair’s sum stays fixed, so the mean is still \(5\). Their deviations become \(-(3+t)\) and \(3+t\). An SD bound of four gives a variance bound of sixteen.
starters.solution:
1. \[(2-t)+5+5+(8+t)=20\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bar{x}=5.\]
  2. \[V(t)=\frac{(-(3+t))^2+0+0+(3+t)^2}{4}=\frac{(t+3)^2}{2}.\]

  3. Both the SD and the bound are non-negative, so

    \[\sigma\le4\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V(t)\le16\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(t+3)^2\le32.\]

  4. The boundary equation has the two real roots

    \[t=-3\pm4\sqrt{2}.\]

    The unrestricted real inequality holds between these roots, including the endpoints.

  5. Intersect with the original domain \(t\ge0\):

    \[0\le t\le4\sqrt{2}-3.\]

    The upper endpoint gives SD exactly \(4\), so it is included.

  6. Since \(2<4\sqrt{2}-3<3\), the allowed integer adjustments are exactly \(0,1,2\). The negative boundary root is not an allowed outward adjustment.

  • 1 mark: identify both changed deviations from the mean.
  • 1 mark: obtain the complete variance expression, including its cross term.
  • 1 mark: convert the non-negative SD bound to a variance bound.
  • 1 mark: solve for both real boundary roots.
  • 1 mark: choose the interval between the roots with equality included.
  • 1 mark: intersect with the original non-negative adjustment domain.
  • 1 mark: list the complete allowed integer set.

revision.body:
Update the count and both moment totals before calculating spread.

Change the complete moment ledger

Use \(n,T=\sum x,Q=\sum x^2\). Replace \(r\) by \(t\):

\[(n,T,Q)\longrightarrow(n,T-r+t,Q-r^2+t^2).\]

Add \(z\): \((n+1,T+z,Q+z^2)\). Remove one \(z\): \((n-1,T-z,Q-z^2)\). Then

\[\mu=\frac{T}{n},\qquad V=\frac{Q}{n}-\mu^2,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{V}.\]

Use the new count. A singleton has zero variance; an empty list has no mean or spread.

Pool two groups or recover a missing group

\[T_i=n_i\mu_i,\qquad Q_i=n_i(V_i+\mu_i^2).\]

For two nonempty disjoint groups, add \(n_i,T_i,Q_i\) on one original scale. Recover a missing group by subtraction, then check feasibility.

\[V=w_AV_A+w_BV_B+w_Aw_B(\mu_A-\mu_B)^2,\]\[w_A=\frac{n_A}{n_A+n_B},\qquad w_B=\frac{n_B}{n_A+n_B}.\]

The last term is the between-group contribution. Decode all groups to common units before pooling; do not average their SDs.

Add one record without changing the SD

\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{n}{n+1}V+\frac{n}{(n+1)^2}(z-\mu)^2.\]

To keep the same SD, require

\[(z-\mu)^2=\frac{n+1}{n}V.\]

For \(V>0\), retain both signs before applying record restrictions. For \(V=0\), only \(z=\mu\) works. Adding \(\mu\) decreases positive variance.

Move a symmetric pair and enforce an SD bound

Move an existing pair \(\mu\pm d\) to \(\mu\pm(d+t)\), with \(d,t\ge0\). The mean stays fixed:

\[V_{\mathrm{new}}=V+\frac{4dt+2t^2}{n}.\]

For an SD limit \(b\ge0\), solve \(V_{\mathrm{new}}\le b^2\), then enforce \(t\ge0\) and all record restrictions.

• Updated records, squares, count and common scale; hidden group feasible?
  • Between-group spread, both addition signs and all bounds included?

orig_9709_s1_var_frequency_synthesis.description: Use exact frequency totals, midpoint estimates and cumulative interpolation for the questions each can answer. Then combine centre and spread information to recover unknown frequencies or missing observations without losing valid branches.

sections.title: When does a frequency table give exact spread?
sections.label: Exact frequency moments
sections.intro:
If each row gives an actual value \(x\) and frequency \(f\), all original records are preserved. Frequencies are non-negative integers and the total count must be positive. Form

\[N=\sum f,\qquad T=\sum fx,\qquad Q=\sum fx^2.\]

Then the exact descriptive summaries are

\[\mu=\frac{T}{N},\qquad V=\frac{Q}{N}-\mu^2,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{V}.\]

The divisor is the number of records, not the number of table rows. A zero-frequency row contributes nothing.

blocks.html: Each row contributes \(fx^2=f(x^2)\) to the sum of squares. Squaring \(fx\) would incorrectly square the frequency as well. The square of the total, \(T^2\), is another different quantity.

blocks.title: Square the data value before applying frequency
blocks.prompt: The values \(-2,0,4\) have frequencies \(2,3,1\), respectively. Find the original total, sum of squares, mean and descriptive SD.
blocks.hint: There are six records. A row contributes its frequency multiplied by the square of its value, including when that value is negative.

blocks.html: When using a calculator, enter the frequencies in its frequency column and choose descriptive SD with the full record count as divisor. Show \(N,T,Q\) and the substitution so your method is visible. Report variance in squared units and SD in the original units.

sections.title: What does a grouped spread estimate actually assume?
sections.label: Grouped midpoint spread
sections.intro:
A grouped table preserves counts but usually loses each record’s position inside its class. For continuous boundaries \(L,U\), use midpoint \(m=\frac{L+U}{2}\). Replace every record in a class by \(m\), then calculate

\[T_m=\sum fm,\qquad Q_m=\sum fm^2,\]\[\widehat{\mu}=\frac{T_m}{N},\qquad\widehat{V}=\frac{Q_m}{N}-\widehat{\mu}^{\,2},\qquad\widehat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\widehat{V}}.\]

These are estimates for the original records. They are exact summaries of the specified midpoint replacement list.

Use frequencies as weights even when widths differ. If a histogram supplies density \(D\) and width \(w\), recover frequency \(f=Dw\) first. Density alone is not the number of records.

blocks.title: Calculate the midpoint estimates
blocks.prompt:
Lengths in centimetres are grouped as follows.

ClassFrequency
\(0\le x<4\)\(5\)
\(4\le x<10\)\(8\)
\(10\le x<18\)\(3\)

Use class midpoints to estimate the mean and descriptive variance. State what these calculations establish about the original data.

options.estimate: Exact for the midpoint replacement list; estimates for the original records.
options.raw: Both are guaranteed exact for the original records.
options.uniform: The variance is the exact variance of a continuous uniform model within every class.

blocks.hint: The midpoints are \(2,7,14\). Weight them by the class frequencies, even though the widths are unequal.
blocks.solution:
1. \[N=16,\quad T_m=5(2)+8(7)+3(14)=108,\]\[Q_m=5(2^2)+8(7^2)+3(14^2)=1000.\]
  2. \[\widehat{\mu}=\frac{108}{16}=\frac{27}{4}\,\mathrm{cm},\]\[\widehat{V}=\frac{1000}{16}-\left(\frac{27}{4}\right)^2=\frac{271}{16}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

  3. These are exact summaries of the list formed by repeating each midpoint its class frequency times. The actual positions inside the classes are unknown, so the original mean and variance are only estimated.

blocks.html: The midpoint method and uniform interpolation are different models. Midpoint moments place each class’s records at its centre. A continuous uniform model spreads the class count across its width for percentile estimates. Midpoint variance is not the exact variance of that continuous model.

In the interactive, equal numbers of records sit at \(m-d\) and \(m+d\) in each class. With \(d\) measured numerically in centimetres, this constructed family has actual mean \(\frac{23}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\) and actual variance \((39+d^2)\,\mathrm{cm}^2\), while its grouped estimates stay fixed. Other within-class arrangements can change the actual mean as well. The construction does not make the midpoint variance a universal lower bound for raw variance.

For these \(40\) constructed raw records, the overall median averages the values at positions \(20\) and \(21\). Raw quartiles are the medians of the lower and upper \(20\) records, retaining both central observations in their respective halves. These exact summaries follow the known records; the interpolated quartiles still follow the separate uniform model.

sections.title: How do I turn percentile ranks into an IQR or cutoff?
sections.label: Percentiles and cutoffs
sections.intro:
Accumulate frequencies at upper class boundaries, starting with zero at the first lower boundary. For a grouped percentile with proportion \(p\), use cumulative level \(r=pN\). The quartile levels are \(\frac{N}{4},\frac{N}{2},\frac{3N}{4}\). These grouped levels are distinct from the course’s median-of-halves rule for a fully known raw list.

Under a uniform-within-class model, join cumulative points by straight segments. In a class of positive frequency \(f\), lower boundary \(L\), width \(w\), and cumulative count \(C\) before the class, the fraction of the class count needed is \(\frac{r-C}{f}\). Move that same fraction of the width:

\[x_r=L+\frac{r-C}{f}w.\]

The IQR is \(Q_3-Q_1\), a difference of data values with the original units.

blocks.html: If \(C(c)\) counts actual records below \(c\), then \(N-C(c)\) counts records at least \(c\). Actual ties at the cutoff matter. In the continuous interpolation model, no count is placed at one exact value, so its model counts above and at least agree. A cutoff exceeded by \(k\) records therefore uses level \(N-k\) under that model.

The cumulative points are \((0,0),\ (5,8),\ (15,28),\ (25,40)\). With \(N=40\), use counts \(10,20,30\) for the quartiles.

\[Q_1\approx6\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad Q_2\approx11\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad Q_3\approx\frac{50}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]\[\mathrm{IQR}\approx\frac{50}{3}-6=\frac{32}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

For eight observations above the cutoff, use cumulative count \(40-8=32\). The estimated upper proportion is \(\frac{8}{40}=\frac15\).

\[c\approx15+\frac{32-28}{12}(25-15)=\frac{55}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

On the straight-segment cumulative model, levels \(10,20,30\) give quartile estimates \(6,11,\frac{50}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}\). Level \(32\) gives the upper-tail cutoff \(\frac{55}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}\).

blocks.title: Convert cumulative levels to lengths
blocks.prompt: Lengths in centimetres have classes \([0,10),[10,20),[20,40)\), with frequencies \(10,25,15\). Use a continuous uniform model within each class and straight-line cumulative interpolation. Estimate the lower and upper quartiles, IQR, and the cutoff exceeded by \(10\) of the \(50\) records in this model.
blocks.hint: The cumulative totals are \(0,10,35,50\). Use levels \(12.5\), \(37.5\) and \(50-10=40\), then interpolate in the relevant class.
blocks.solution:
1. \[Q_1\approx10+\frac{\frac{25}{2}-10}{25}(10)=11\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
  2. \[Q_3\approx20+\frac{\frac{75}{2}-35}{15}(20)=\frac{70}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
  3. \[\mathrm{IQR}\approx\frac{70}{3}-11=\frac{37}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  4. Ten above means cumulative level \(40\) under the stated continuous model:

    \[c\approx20+\frac{40-35}{15}(20)=\frac{80}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

blocks.html:
An empty class produces a horizontal segment. Never divide by its zero frequency: if a target equals that flat level, every cutoff on the segment matches it unless another convention selects one. For example, a segment with cumulative count \(9\) from \(6\) to \(10\) has all those cutoffs at level \(9\).

The first and last plotted boundaries do not identify the actual minimum and maximum. A freehand cumulative curve gives graphical estimates at its reading precision; use the straight-line formula only when that interpolation model is specified. Use class boundaries implied by the stated rounding or recording rule, and do not automatically close a genuine gap.

sections.title: How can a spread condition determine a missing frequency?
sections.label: Reverse a frequency
sections.intro:
Write the count, total and sum of squares in terms of the unknown frequency before using the variance equation. The same unknown may appear in all three quantities. If the question supplies SD, square it to obtain variance.

Solve the resulting equation and retain every branch. A frequency must be an integer and must be non-negative, or positive if stated. Also require \(N>0\). Check each surviving table in the original variance formula and any mean condition; do not select a branch just because it looks simpler.

blocks.title: Reject a fractional frequency
blocks.prompt: The value \(0\) occurs \(k\) times and the value \(5\) occurs twice, where \(k\) is a positive integer. The descriptive variance is \(4\). Find every valid \(k\), then the corresponding mean.
blocks.hint: The total count is \(k+2\), while the original total and sum of squares are \(10\) and \(50\). Keep both algebraic roots until checking the frequency condition.
blocks.solution:
1. \[4=\frac{50}{k+2}-\left(\frac{10}{k+2}\right)^2.\]
  2. \[4(k+2)^2=50k\Longrightarrow2k^2-17k+8=0.\]
  3. \[(2k-1)(k-8)=0\Longrightarrow k=\frac{1}{2}\text{ or }k=8.\]

  4. A frequency must be a whole number, so only \(k=8\) remains. It gives

    \[N=10,\quad\mu=1,\quad V=\frac{50}{10}-1^2=4.\]

sections.title: How do mean and variance reveal two missing records?
sections.label: Recover two observations
sections.intro:
Use the final number of records, including the two missing ones. From a stated mean and descriptive variance, reconstruct

\[T=N\mu,\qquad Q=N(V+\mu^2).\]

Subtract the known records to obtain \(a+b=S\) and \(a^2+b^2=R\). Then

\[ab=\frac{S^2-R}{2},\qquad z^2-Sz+\frac{S^2-R}{2}=0.\]

The roots are the missing observation values. When they differ, both assignments to the labels \(a,b\) remain possible until an order condition selects one.

Real roots require \((a-b)^2=2R-S^2\ge0\). Equality gives two equal values, which cannot satisfy a strict order such as \(a<b\). Apply integer, sign and other context restrictions to the values themselves, then restore both original moments.

blocks.title: Keep the labels until an order condition selects a pair
blocks.prompt: The six observations are \(0,2,4,6,a,b\). Their mean is \(4\) and descriptive variance is \(\frac{25}{3}\). Find every labelled pair \((a,b)\). Then give the pair satisfying \(a>b\).
blocks.hint: Recover the complete total and sum of squares first. Subtract the four known records, then form a quadratic whose roots are the two missing values.
blocks.solution:
1. \[T=6(4)=24,\qquad Q=6\left(\frac{25}{3}+4^2\right)=146.\]
  2. \[a+b=24-12=12,\qquad a^2+b^2=146-56=90.\]
  3. \[ab=\frac{12^2-90}{2}=27,\qquad z^2-12z+27=(z-3)(z-9).\]

  4. The labelled pairs are \((3,9)\) and \((9,3)\). Both give the stated total and sum of squares. The condition \(a>b\) selects \((9,3)\).

glossary.definition: The number of original records represented by a table row.
A total such as \(\sum fx\) or \(\sum fx^2\), calculated from known observation values and their frequencies.
A calculation that replaces each observation by the midpoint of its class.
A summary calculated from grouped information and a stated model, without knowing the original within-class positions.
A model that distributes a class’s frequency evenly across its width, making the cumulative segment straight.
The cumulative count \(pN\) corresponding to a proportion \(p\) of the total records.
The data-value difference \(Q_3-Q_1\), expressed in the original measurement units.
A data value with a stated count or proportion above it; strict versus inclusive inequalities matter for actual ties.
A horizontal cumulative segment corresponding to an empty class; its count level may match an interval of cutoffs.
Different assignments of the recovered values to the unknown record labels, retained until a stated condition selects one.

examples.title: Use frequencies to recover exact moments
examples.question: The values \(1,3,6\) occur \(2,4,2\) times, respectively. Calculate the exact mean, descriptive variance and SD.
solution:
\[\sigma=\frac{\sqrt{51}}{4}.\]

These are exact because each row specifies an actual observation value and its number of occurrences.

examples.title: Estimate spread from unequal-width classes
examples.question:
Estimate the mean and descriptive SD of these lengths using class midpoints.

Length \(x\) in \(\mathrm{cm}\)Frequency
\(0\le x<5\)\(8\)
\(5\le x<15\)\(20\)
\(15\le x<25\)\(12\)
solution: The widths are \(5,10,10\), and the midpoints are \(\frac{5}{2},10,20\). The weights remain the frequencies \(8,20,12\).
The values are exact for the midpoint replacement list and estimates for the original lengths. Unequal class widths do not justify replacing the frequencies by histogram heights.

examples.title: Find quartiles and an upper-tail cutoff
examples.question:
Use a continuous uniform model within each class of this table, joining cumulative points by straight segments. Estimate the quartiles, IQR and the cutoff exceeded by \(8\) of the \(40\) records under that model.

Length \(x\) in \(\mathrm{cm}\)Frequency
\(0\le x<5\)\(8\)
\(5\le x<15\)\(20\)
\(15\le x<25\)\(12\)
solution:
\[\mathrm{IQR}\approx\frac{50}{3}-6=\frac{32}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Subtract the two estimated lengths, not their cumulative levels.

Eight above corresponds to cumulative level \(40-8=32\), which is also the \(80\)th percentile level:

\[c\approx15+\frac{32-28}{12}(10)=\frac{55}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The arithmetic is exact within this interpolation model; the original-data percentiles remain estimates.

examples.title: A spread condition can leave two frequency branches
examples.question: The value \(0\) has frequency \(k\), and the value \(6\) has frequency \(2\), where \(k\) is a positive integer. The descriptive variance is \(8\). Find all possible \(k\), then select the value if the mean exceeds \(3\).
solution:
\[N=k+2,\qquad T=12,\qquad Q=72.\]

The unknown frequency changes the denominator as well as the list.
Both frequency tables satisfy the original spread condition. Requiring \(\mu>3\) selects \(k=1\).

examples.title: Recover two observations from centre and spread
examples.question: The six observations \(2,3,5,6,a,b\) have mean \(5\) and descriptive variance \(\frac{20}{3}\). Find every labelled pair \((a,b)\), then select the pair if \(a<b\).
solution:
The known records have total \(16\) and sum of squares \(74\). Therefore,

\[a+b=14,\qquad a^2+b^2=116.\]

\[ab=\frac{14^2-116}{2}=40.\]

Each missing value is a root of

\[z^2-14z+40=(z-4)(z-10)=0.\]
The labelled pairs are \((4,10)\) and \((10,4)\). The condition \(a<b\) selects \((4,10)\).

extraPractice.title: Count repeated values in both moments
extraPractice.prompt: A frequency table has values \(1,3,7\) with respective frequencies \(2,3,1\). Find the count, mean, descriptive variance and SD exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Each frequency counts repeated copies of its value. The second-moment column is \(fx^2\), not \((fx)^2\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N=2+3+1=6,\qquad T=2(1)+3(3)+1(7)=18.\]
  2. \[Q=2(1^2)+3(3^2)+1(7^2)=2+27+49=78.\]
  3. \[\bar{x}=\frac{18}{6}=3,\qquad V=\frac{78}{6}-3^2=4,\qquad\sigma=2.\]

  4. These are exact summaries of the raw list \(1,1,3,3,3,7\). Squaring the frequency-weighted products would instead count the repetitions incorrectly.

extraPractice.title: Use frequencies for unequal-width moment estimates
extraPractice.prompt:
Continuous lengths \(x\), in centimetres, are grouped as follows.

ClassFrequency
\(0\le x<6\)\(2\)
\(6\le x<10\)\(5\)
\(10\le x<20\)\(3\)

Using class midpoints, estimate the mean, descriptive variance and SD. Give unrounded values for this midpoint model and identify what they tell you about the unknown raw data.

fields.label: How should these values be interpreted?

options.estimates: Exact for the midpoint model; estimates of the unknown raw summaries.
options.raw: Exact raw summaries because the total count is known.
options.density: Invalid unless the frequencies are replaced by densities.

extraPractice.hint: The midpoints are \(3,8,15\). Frequency remains the weight even though the class widths differ.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[N=10,\qquad T_m=2(3)+5(8)+3(15)=91.\]
  2. \[Q_m=2(3^2)+5(8^2)+3(15^2)=1013.\]
  3. \[\widehat{\mu}=\frac{91}{10}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\widehat{V}=\frac{1013}{10}-\left(\frac{91}{10}\right)^2=\frac{1849}{100}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  4. \[\widehat{\sigma}=\frac{43}{10}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  5. The midpoint replacement gives exact values for its representative list, but the original positions inside each interval are unknown. Frequency density sets histogram height; it does not replace frequency in these moment sums.

extraPractice.title: Interpolate values, including a cutoff with a given upper count
extraPractice.prompt:
A cumulative frequency table for continuous measurements is

Boundary \(x\)\(0\)\(10\)\(20\)\(40\)
Count below \(x\)\(0\)\(6\)\(24\)\(30\)

Use a continuous model with uniform spread in each class and straight segments between these points. Estimate both quartiles, the IQR, the ninetieth percentile and a cutoff exceeded by nine observations under this model.

Separately, another continuous cumulative model is flat at count \(15\) throughout \([10,20]\). Which cutoffs in that interval satisfy \(C(c)=15\)?
extraPractice.hint: Use cumulative targets \(\frac{N}{4}\), \(\frac{3N}{4}\), \(0.9N\) and \(N-9\). These are counts to locate on the cumulative axis, not the requested measurement values.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Here \(N=30\); the class frequencies are \(6,18,6\). The quartile targets are \(\frac{15}{2}\) and \(\frac{45}{2}\), both inside the middle class.

  2. \[\widehat{Q}_1=10+\frac{\frac{15}{2}-6}{18}(10)=\frac{65}{6},\]
  3. \[\widehat{Q}_3=10+\frac{\frac{45}{2}-6}{18}(10)=\frac{115}{6},\qquad\widehat{\mathrm{IQR}}=\frac{115-65}{6}=\frac{25}{3}.\]
  4. \[\widehat{x}_{0.9}=20+\frac{27-24}{6}(20)=30.\]

  5. Nine above the cutoff means cumulative target \(30-9=21\) in this continuous model:

    \[\widehat{c}=10+\frac{21-6}{18}(10)=\frac{55}{3}.\]

  6. On the separate plateau, every point of \([10,20]\) has cumulative count \(15\). That equality alone does not select one cutoff. Do not divide by a zero class frequency or choose the midpoint without a stated rule.

extraPractice.title: Recover frequencies and reject an unattainable variance
extraPractice.prompt: The values \(1,3,5\) have frequencies \(p,4,q\), where \(p,q\) are non-negative integers. The mean is \(3\) and descriptive variance is \(2\). Find \(p,q\) and the total count. Separately, could any finite choices of \(p,q\), with the same values, middle frequency \(4\) and mean \(3\), give variance exactly \(4\)?

fields.label: Can the separate variance equal four?

options.no: No finite frequencies satisfy the resulting equation.
options.large: Yes: choosing sufficiently large frequencies makes it exactly four.
options.negative: Yes: allow a negative frequency to balance the table.

extraPractice.hint: The mean equation relates \(p\) and \(q\). Then calculate the total squared deviation from the known mean \(3\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[p+12+5q=3(p+4+q)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=q.\]

  2. The squared deviations are \(4,0,4\), so

    \[V=\frac{4p+4q}{p+q+4}=\frac{8p}{2p+4}.\]
  3. \[2=\frac{8p}{2p+4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad4p+8=8p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=q=2.\]
  4. \[N=2+4+2=8.\]

    The frequencies are non-negative integers, and the table has the stated mean and variance.

  5. For the separate variance claim,

    \[4=\frac{8p}{2p+4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad8p+16=8p,\]

    which is impossible. Increasing finite frequencies does not turn that contradiction into an equality.

extraPractice.title: Recover both labelled missing-value branches
extraPractice.prompt: Two real observations \(a,b\) are added to \(3,5,8,10\). The six observations have mean \(7\) and descriptive variance \(\frac{20}{3}\). Find every ordered pair \((a,b)\), then select the pair if \(a<b\). Separately, could the same four known values and final mean \(7\) instead have final variance \(5\) after adding two real observations?

fields.label: Is the separate variance proposal possible?

options.no: No: the required sum of squares of the two missing values is too small.
options.yes: Yes: choose a negative observation to reduce its square.
options.one: Yes: it is enough to satisfy the mean.

extraPractice.hint: The mean gives the missing sum. The variance gives the missing sum of squares. For two real numbers with sum \(S\), their sum of squares must be at least \(\frac{S^2}{2}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[T=6(7)=42,\qquad a+b=42-(3+5+8+10)=16.\]
  2. \[Q=6\left(\frac{20}{3}+7^2\right)=334,\qquad a^2+b^2=334-198=136.\]
  3. \[ab=\frac{16^2-136}{2}=60,\qquad z^2-16z+60=(z-6)(z-10)=0.\]

  4. Both labelled assignments \((6,10)\) and \((10,6)\) satisfy the original moments. The condition \(a<b\) selects \((6,10)\). The additional record equal to \(10\) is still a separate observation.

  5. The separate proposal would give

    \[Q=6(5+49)=324,\qquad a^2+b^2=324-198=126.\]

    But the unchanged missing sum \(16\) requires

    \[a^2+b^2\ge\frac{16^2}{2}=128.\]

    Thus no real pair can meet that proposal.

starters.title: Keep midpoint estimates separate from a reversed percentile
starters.question: Sixteen continuous readings \(x\), in centimetres, are grouped into \([0,4)\), \([4,10)\), \([10,18)\), with frequencies \(4,8,4\). Estimate the mean and SD using class midpoints. A calibration changes each reading to \(y=50-2x\), with \(y\) also measured in centimetres. Estimate the new mean and SD. For percentiles, use a continuous model uniform within each original class: estimate the new IQR and a value of \(y\) exceeded by four of the sixteen readings under this model. Give unrounded values for the stated models.
starters.hint: Use midpoints for moment estimates and uniform interpolation for percentiles. The negative scale reverses order: a large calibrated reading comes from a small original reading.
starters.solution:
1. The original class midpoints are \(2,7,14\), giving

    \[T_m=4(2)+8(7)+4(14)=120,\]\[Q_m=4(2^2)+8(7^2)+4(14^2)=1192.\]
  2. \[\widehat{\mu}_x=\frac{120}{16}=\frac{15}{2}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\widehat{V}_x=\frac{1192}{16}-\left(\frac{15}{2}\right)^2=\frac{73}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  3. \[\widehat{\sigma}_x=\frac{\sqrt{73}}{2}\,\mathrm{cm},\quad\widehat{\mu}_y=50-2\left(\frac{15}{2}\right)=35\,\mathrm{cm},\quad\widehat{\sigma}_y=2\left(\frac{\sqrt{73}}{2}\right)=\sqrt{73}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  4. For the continuous uniform model, cumulative targets \(4\) and \(12\) fall at class boundaries, so \(\widehat{Q}_{1,x}=4\) and \(\widehat{Q}_{3,x}=10\). Hence

    \[\widehat{\mathrm{IQR}}_y=2(10-4)=12\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  5. The four greatest calibrated readings correspond to the four smallest original readings. More explicitly,

    \[y>c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x<\frac{50-c}{2}.\]

    The original cumulative target is therefore \(4\), whose interpolated cutoff is \(4\).

  6. \[\frac{50-c}{2}=4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=42\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  7. The midpoint mean and SD and the interpolated quartiles estimate unknown raw summaries. The cutoff is a useful boundary exception: the table itself puts exactly four raw readings below \(4\), so exactly four calibrated readings exceed \(42\), even without uniformity. Midpoint replacement and uniform interpolation remain distinct models.

starters.title: Use both frequency branches before adding a new record
starters.question: A frequency table has numerical values \(0\) and \(4\), with respective frequencies \(k\) and \(3\), where \(k\) is a positive integer. Its descriptive variance is \(3\). Find every possible \(k\). Additional information says the mean is less than \(2\): select the frequency and find the mean. For this selected dataset, find every real observation \(z\) that can be added without changing the SD. Finally, select the addition if every record must be non-negative.
starters.hint: The count is \(k+3\), total \(12\) and sum of squares \(48\). Retain both frequency roots before using the mean condition. Then apply the one-record variance identity to the selected dataset.
starters.solution:
1. \[3=\frac{48}{k+3}-\left(\frac{12}{k+3}\right)^2=\frac{48k}{(k+3)^2}.\]
  2. \[(k+3)^2=16k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k^2-10k+9=(k-1)(k-9)=0.\]

  3. Both \(k=1\) and \(k=9\) are valid positive integer frequencies. Their means are \(3\) and \(1\), respectively. The condition \(\mu<2\) selects \(k=9\), giving \(n=12\), \(\mu=1\), \(V=3\).

  4. Equal SDs require equal variances. After adding one observation,

    \[3=\frac{12}{13}(3)+\frac{12}{169}(z-1)^2.\]
  5. \[(z-1)^2=\frac{13}{4}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=1\pm\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}.\]

  6. Both real additions preserve the SD \(\sqrt{3}\). Since \(\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}>1\), the lower branch is negative. Requiring every observation to be non-negative therefore selects \(z=1+\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\).

revision.body:
Choose the correct model before calculating a spread or percentile.

Exact frequencies: weight both moments

\[N=\sum f>0,\quad T=\sum fx,\quad Q=\sum fx^2.\]\[\mu=\frac{T}{N},\qquad V=\frac{Q}{N}-\mu^2,\qquad\sigma=\sqrt{V}.\]

Frequencies count repetitions: use \(fx^2\), not \((fx)^2\). Unknown frequencies must be non-negative integers.

Grouped moments: replace each class by its midpoint

Use \(m=\frac{L+U}{2}\) with weights \(f\):

\[\widehat{\mu}=\frac{\sum fm}{N},\qquad\widehat{V}=\frac{\sum fm^2}{N}-\widehat{\mu}^{\,2}.\]

These are exact for the midpoint model and estimates of the raw summaries. Histogram area gives \(f\); density is not the moment weight. Class boundaries need not be observed extremes.

Percentiles: interpolate a cumulative count

Assume a continuous model uniform within each class. For target \(pN\) inside a positive-frequency class:

\[\widehat{x}_p=L+\frac{pN-C}{f}\,w.\]

Here \(L\) is its lower boundary, \(C\) the count below \(L\), \(f\) its frequency and \(w\) its width. For an upper count \(k\), use target \(N-k\). Subtract quartile values for IQR, not their ranks.

A flat cumulative segment can give an interval of cutoffs for a stated count. Do not divide by zero or invent a unique cutoff.

Reverse moments: retain every feasible branch

Build mean and variance equations from \(N,T,Q\); check all frequency roots in the original table. For two missing real observations, let \(S=a+b\) and \(R=a^2+b^2\). Then

\[ab=\frac{S^2-R}{2},\qquad a,b=\frac{S\pm\sqrt{2R-S^2}}{2}.\]

Real solutions require \(2R\ge S^2\). Include both labelled assignments unless a stated order or context removes one.
